Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege concerning an editorial in the Financial Post of May 13, 1961, which in my opinion is irresponsible, somewhat libellous and in at least one respect not true. The editorial reads:
It's outrageous that 469 divorce petitions are stalled in parliament, and likely to remain stalled indefinitely, by a blockading operation conducted by two M.P.'s.
Most Canadians agree that these petitions, all coming from Quebec and Newfoundland, should not [DOT]be parliament's business at all. A federal court should handle them if these two provinces are not willing to empower their own courts to dissolve marriages.
But years of argument have not yet persuaded any Canadian government to sponsor reform in the system; and there is not the slightest immediate chance of reform.
In these circumstances, the continuation of last year's indiscriminate filibuster against all divorce bills by two C.C.F.'ers, Frank Howard and Arnold Peters, is a cheap political stunt. It's a callous and brutal stunt because it will force 469 Canadian couples to stay unhappily married when, presumably, there is conclusive evidence that they ought to be divorced.
I would point out that the so-called "blockading operation", as it is termed in the editorial, is occasioned not by any activity of the hon. member for Timiskaming or myself but is occasioned in the first instance by the refusal of the Senate to deal with a particular bill that was sent to it-

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the time of the national exercise on civil defence or just prior thereto I stated that I would give a statement regarding the findings and the experiences of those who participated in that exercise. The purpose of the exercise was not only to practice and test the emergency measures which are necessary for national survival and continuity of government, but in particular to identify gaps in existing plans and preparations.
I think the initial report indicates that the exercise served its purpose adequately. Sirens were sounded in a number of communities across the country. Siren coverage is rapidly being increased and many more areas will, within the next year, have these warning devices.
The early stages of the exercise in Ottawa went as planned and certain emergency procedures of government were practised. The signal authorizing the sounding of the alert took only 39 seconds from the time it was sent to the provincial centres by the federal warning centre until the last acknowledgement was received from the provincial warning centres.
The exercise in the central headquarters at Camp Petawawa showed considerable improvement in preparations and capabilities over 1960, and revealed that in an emergency the basic elements of government could be operated. However, I would be less than frank if I did not point out that the efficiency of the operation was less than is requisite, and much remains to be done in the fields of departmental emergency planning, advance preparation of executive orders and policy directives, staff training, organization of staff to work effectively in emergency

Civil Defence
facilities, and further improvement in communications. These problems will receive urgent attention.
First reports from the regional centres which were set up indicate that the exercise went well in the provinces. Federal personnel close to the maximum numbers planned participated. Provincial participation varied considerably, depending upon the stage of provincial planning and preparation in this field. Provincial governments were represented in most provinces, and in so far as the federal government was concerned it was represented in most of the provinces either by cabinet ministers or by parliamentary secretaries.
At the central headquarters at Petawawa several federal ministers were at work in connection with their emergency assignments. I should like to say a special word of commendation for the observers, the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) and the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch).
Many hundreds of persons in the service of government at all levels played an active part. At the central headquarters alone almost 200 took part. Besides the activity by federal and provincial personnel at regional headquarters in the provinces, some 500 municipalities throughout Canada also took part.
Many gaps were revealed in the plans and preparations. I feel, however, that a considerable advance in the knowledge of the problems to be faced has been achieved, and that all concerned are better prepared to play their part should a real emergency arise. So far as the gaps are concerned, every effort will be made to fill them and to remove any evidence of weaknesses revealed during the course of the exercise.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if, unfortunately, civil defence is necessary in the world in which we live, it is important that it should be planned and organized as effectively as possible. As the Prime Minister has pointed out, the operation in question has shown that there is a great deal to be done in that regard. Civil defence is important, but policies in all countries to make civil defence unnecessary are even more important.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that it is the policy of the government to endeavour to establish an organization for civil defence and to spend considerable money on it, it is perhaps a good thing that the recent exercise referred to was held. I cannot help but say that the Prime Minister must have been on an exercise different from the one I was on, in view of what he said a few moments ago.

I was grateful for the opportunity of serving as an observer. There is no opportunity at this time to discuss all the experiences of the exercise, but in my estimation the exercise disclosed not only many minor but many major gaps. I was interested in knowing that the attack was supposed to be realistic. I gathered that from the statement made by the Prime Minister the day previous to the exercise. The attack was to be realistic in order to demonstrate what might happen under certain circumstances. The attack was all by manned bombers except for the latter portion, during which two missiles were discharged.
The major gap disclosed by the operation was this. Outside of the few cabinet ministers, parliamentary secretaries, and two private members from the opposition, the government and the House of Commons were completely wiped out. That may be a good thing.
That is your only chance.

It is obvious, on the basis of this realistic exercise, that there should be considerable discussion of it in this chamber.
I	hope when certain estimates are before the house all hon. members will participate in a discussion of this subject. On behalf of this group I take the position that we are not supposed to keep to ourselves exactly what we observed, especially in terms of gaps in the operation, but that these things should be mentioned and discussed.
In commenting on the remarks of the Prime Minister I feel I must say that something is definitely wrong in this country and in the world if we have to have civil defence. Let us hope that sanity will prevail and that something will be done as speedily as possible in other fields so that our money, effort and brains can be directed to the introduction of useful and productive measures and policies.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: I cannot add anything to what has been said, Mr. Speaker. Both the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Vancouver East mentioned the fact that every effort should be made to bring about peace, thereby denying the necessity of civil defence. That is not only their view but the view of this government, which has pressed very strongly to bring about disarmament while at the same time having to maintain defences until disarmament is attained.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I should say a word at this time respecting Laos. On May
II	the international supervisory commission for Laos was able to report to the United

Kingdom and Soviet governments, as cochairmen of the Geneva conference of 1954, that the principal parties to the recent hostilities had ordered their troops to cease fire from 8 a.m. local time on May 3, and that since that time there has been a general and demonstrable cessation of hostilities. The commission is satisfied that a state of de facto cease fire exists throughout Laos.
Despite the commission's report, which was available last Friday, the opening of the conference has been delayed because of disagreement over the seating of Pathet Lao representatives on an equal footing with the representatives of the government headed by Souvanna Phouma, which is recognized by the communist powers, and the royal government of Vientiane. Some countries have taken the position that to concede equal status to the Pathet Lao would prejudge the central issue of the conference and place them on a footing to which as representatives of a paramilitary organization they were not entitled.
There have been suggestions that the conference should be allowed to proceed, dealing first with such practical matters as the question of the cease fire, leaving time for the Laotian parties to agree among themselves on a government for Laos and representation at the conference. Another suggestion has been that any delegation should be permitted to invite any Laotian group to participate in the conference as observers without prejudice to the ultimate composition of the government to be formed in connection with a political settlement. While this formula was acceptable to the principal powers, it has not yet been * agreed to by the representatives of the royal government, and consequently there is still doubt as to when the conference will be able to begin its work.
In view of all the circumstances I think I should advise the house that the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who expected to return to Canada tomorrow, will be remaining in Geneva, and that the earliest possible date for his return, short of a complete breakdown of the conference, will be the end of the week. He had a number of appointments here during the latter part of the week, I believe on Thursday, Friday and Saturday. Those appointments will be cancelled in view of the situation prevailing at Geneva.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fullon (Minister of Justice) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-92, to amend the Criminal Code (capital murder).

subtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to revise the provisions of the Criminal Code dealing with the death penalty and also the provisions dealing with the trial of a person charged with an offence for which the penalty is death.
The provisions relate primarily to the crime of murder, and the effect is to divide murder into two types, capital and noncapital. Under the proposed legislation the death penalty will attach only to murder of a planned and deliberate character, or to killing in the course of committing a crime of a nature importing the elements of deliberation or stealth. In such case only the person who committed the act resulting in death, or who counselled or procured it, would be subject to the death penalty.
The bill also makes changes in the provisions regarding the plea to be entered by a person charged with an offence for which the penalty may be death, and provides automatic review by the court of appeal of any case where the death penalty has been imposed. There are other consequential and related provisions.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Prime Minister in his capacity as Secretary of State for External Affairs. In the light of a recent decision by the United States courts limiting to the amount of $8,300 the liability of an air carrier on an international flight, under the Warsaw convention to which Canada is a signatory, as reported in the Financial Post of May 13, does the government intend to make representations through its delegates at I.C.A.O. or at some other international level to amend the Warsaw convention?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO AMENDMENT OF WARSAW CONVENTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman gave me notice of his question. The Warsaw convention limits the liability of an air carrier on an international flight to the amount of $8,300. On August 16, 1956 Canada signed the Hague protocol, which was opened for signature on September 28, 1955. The purpose of the Hague protocol, which incidentally requires ratification by 30 states
I Mr. Fulton.]
before coming into effect, is to double the amount of the liability established under the Warsaw convention. To date only 19 states have ratified the convention. As the house will know, five and a half years have gone by from the time it was opened for signature.
A factor having an influence on the government's decision to ratify will be the likelihood of sufficient countries ratifying the protocol to bring it into effect. However, I can say that ratification is under consideration. Nevertheless, I know the hon. gentleman will realize that when only 19 of the requisite minimum of 30 have actually ratified, there is not too much hope of the protocol coming into effect.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO AMENDMENT OF WARSAW CONVENTION
speechtext: If I may, I should like to ask this additional question. Does the Prime Minister not think that if Canada were to ratify it, that might lead others to follow its example?

Hon. E. D. Fulton (for the Minister of Agriculture), moved the second reading of Bill No. C-89, to amend the Criminal Code (race meetings).
He said: Section 178 of the Criminal Code provides that parimutuel betting may be conducted on horse racing tracks if the parimutuel betting is under the supervision of an officer appointed by the Minister of Agriculture. The section also stipulates the amount of racing which may be conducted by a racing association each year. The purpose of this bill is to amend the present provisions of the act with respect to the number of days of running racing which an association may conduct and the number of trotting races each day.
With respect to running races, an association may, under the present provisions of the section, hold one meet of 14 consecutive legal racing days or two meets of up to seven days each, with a minimum of 20 days between the two meets. While this permits an association to conduct 14 days of racing, the provision that if two meets are held neither shall consist of more than seven racing days has, in some instances, prevented an association from taking advantage of the authorized 14 days of racing. If, for example, an association scheduled a first meeting of four racing days, the second meeting would be restricted to seven racing days, making a total of only 11 such days of racing.
The proposed amendment would permit an association to schedule either one meeting of 14 days or two meetings of any length so long as the combined total of the two meetings does not exceed 14 days. The amendment merely provides more flexibility to associations in scheduling their race meetings. It does not increase the amount of racing which each association is now authorized to conduct, and the present provision that there shall not be more than eight races on each day continues in effect.
The second part of the amendment deals with trotting and pacing races. The present provisions with respect to the number of events which can be conducted in one day is rather complicated, with varying provisions for races, heats and dashes.
In trotting race parlance a dash is a complete event within itself. Races may be made up of a varying number of heats, with the

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
same horses racing in each heat. The section at present authorizes four combinations of races, heats and dashes in any one racing day. There may be eight races or dashes, which is a total of eight events; or there may be two dashes and four heat races of two heats each, which is a total of ten events; or there may be four heat races of three heats each; which is a total of 12 events; or there may be six heat races of two heats each, which is also a total of 12 events.
This authority for varying combinations of dashes, races and heats has proven to be cumbersome and to create difficulties both for racing associations and for the administration. The purpose of the proposed amendment is to simplify the authority for the number of authorized races and to provide that not more than ten races, or events, will be held in any one day. Racing associations will then be free to adjust their scheduling of races, heats and dashes within that total authority. As in the case of the amendment with respect to running races, there is no increase in the total number of racing events which are now authorized under the section.
In this matter we are, of course, concerned with the humane factor with respect to the horses to the same extent as with the amount of parimutuel betting which is authorized. Since the amendments will not increase the number of events now authorized, but merely provide for more flexibility in scheduling those events, it is considered that both interests are adequately protected in the amendments.
Mr. Speaker, before resuming my seat I think I should simply say that traditionally the responsibility for legislation dealing with this part of the Criminal Code-that is, that part concerned with parimutuel betting and horse racing-has been that of the Minister of Agriculture. The fact that I am speaking today on second reading should not be taken as any departure from that principle. I am speaking on behalf of the Minister of Agriculture, in whose name the bill stands, during his absence in the furtherance of his productive efforts to sell more Canadian wheat.

speechtext:
When this debate closed at ten o'clock several weeks ago I had just been challenged by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River on two points. The first was with reference to the word "rationalization" which I had used, and the need for rationalization in railway operations in this country. He wanted to know what I meant by that. Then he challenged

me to indicate what rationalization would mean in terms of the number of jobs available.
There was a definition in today's issue of the Globe and Mail of the word "rationalization". They said it implies rational or reasonable scientific organization of industry to ensure the best use of labour, material and the machinery of production. The editorial goes on to say that this just means the reign of common sense. I suggest to the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River that if he will look at the statistics for the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific railways he will discover that since 1956 approximately 25,000 jobs have disappeared on the Canadian National Railways and approximately 16,000 jobs have disappeared on the Canadian Pacific Railway.
Now, this surely underlines the importance of some kind of analysis to ascertain where the railways are going. Whether or not the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River likes it, railway jobs are disappearing. I insist that what we need to find out is the rate of attrition, and some means of restoring some stability for the railway employees as a whole. The productivity increase resulting from the use of new equipment means fewer jobs. Surely we can stage these changes so they mean less dislocation than we have seen. It is not a question of saying to the railways that they cannot lay off any more men; the men need jobs. This is going to happen, but it could be put on a reasonable basis. It seems to me that the railways, the unions and the government could consult together to see if these changes could not be put on a reasonable basis.
It seems to me that the MacPherson commission report, which has been tabled since we were last discussing the matter, has given the railways a breathing space of perhaps five to eight years in which they can adjust to these new conditions. However, let no member of the house deceive himself; the MacPherson commission and its recommendations, in themselves, are not going to have any effect of lessening this trend toward a decline in jobs. Any member who has had a divisional point in his constituency is aware of the fact that the use of new equipment is having an effect on employment.
I insist that this is one of the things at which we have to look in connection with the C.N.R., and try to find out from Mr. Gordon when he is before the committee what arrangements are being made to stage these lay-offs and this decline in the working force. The figures are startling to anyone who realizes that the Canadian Pacific and Canadian National railways between them in the last four years-this is not counting 1961-

have seen the loss of employment opportunities for over 40,000 people. This represents a healthy chunk of our working force, when you recognize that about five years ago almost 200,000 people were employed by the railways and within another five years we are likely to be down to about 100,000. This gives you some idea of the impact on the country.
One of the things about which we want to hear from Mr. Gordon when he appears before this committee is this matter of the Canadian National getting into the trucking business. A little over a year ago the Canadian National announced that it had purchased four truck lines. The thing that bothers me is that over the year-this is as I understand it-not a single one of these deals has been completed. I have information that indicates that several of these lines are losing money at the rate of $40,000 to $50,000 a month. We want the background information as to how the Canadian National got into this trucking business, and why they went into it in the way they did by using such different methods from those followed by the Canadian Pacific Railway in connection with Smith Transport.
There are countless questions that I think Mr. Gordon will be facing. I only hope that all members of the committee will try to find out where the Canadian National Railway is going in such fields as trucking and employment. I am sure the hon. member for Laurier will join in these deliberations. We should like to know whether we can ever hope for anything better than these huge deficits Mr. Gordon and his management seem to keep building up.
The last point I would mention is the need for a more thorough explanation of the change in the pension system that was introduced by Canadian National Railways this year. It seems to me from my information that this is somewhat of a bookkeeping entry that makes the financial statement of the railway look about $10 million better than it actually is.
During the last few weeks, Mr. Speaker, I have spent a great deal of time reading over the last 10 committee reports when Mr. Gordon appeared before the committee. We have had some very able members of parliament, including the Minister of Justice and the hon. member for York West, who when they were in opposition seemed to have a great time having a go at Mr. Gordon. In the past there has been a very keen interest displayed by opposition members, but it seems to me that in those 10 years Mr. Gordon has always managed to play a superior Hamlet to that of the members of parliament.
This may be what one would expect because, after all, in money terms, he seems
Freight Rates Reduction Act to be worth seven and half times what each one of us is worth. I call on all members of the committee to use all their zeal to see if we cannot this year get a little deeper into the roots of the Canadian National Railways to find out why this railway is not doing better than it is, despite the fact it has had this vigorous, dramatic, and I might almost say romantic leadership since 1950.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sorry to say that I have not as yet received my file on this subject. However, the committee has seen the wording of the resolution as it appears on the order paper. The last time the Freight Rates Reduction Act was amended my predecessor, the then minister of transport, moved for an extension of that act of 12 months and an increase of $15 million. The reason for that amendment was that the government had decided that the whole matter of the railways would have to be reviewed by a commission known as the MacPherson commission which was to make a complete survey of the situation of railroading in Canada. The MacPherson commission started its sittings, and even at that time my predecessor hoped it would be in a position to make a final report within 12 months. Unfortunately, however, for various reasons this report could not be produced within that time. That was the reason this Freight Rates Reduction Act was extended.
The first volume of the MacPherson commission report came before the public only a few weeks ago. At that time we made sure that the shippers in Canada and the Canadian public would not be hurt by the fact that the MacPherson commission report had been produced so late. Also, as hon. members know, what was produced was only the first volume of that report; there are still two other volumes to come. The purpose of the Freight Rates Reduction Act, as the committee knows, was to reduce, first of all by 7 per cent, the

Freight Rates Reduction Act freight rate increase which had been requested by the railways and had been agreed to by the board of transport commissioners.
This decision of the board of transport commissioners had been appealed by eight of the Canadian provinces. Following that appeal the government decided to bring down this bill. This bill had for its main purpose the provision of $20 million to the railways to permit them to effect a reduction of no less than 7 per cent, which made the previous increase not more than 10 per cent. In actual practice, after the board of transport commissioners had time to assess the real impact of this reduction of $20 million they made a decision to further reduce this freight rate increase by another 2 per cent. As a result shippers were to pay only 8 per cent because of this further reduction.
This further amendment to the Freight Rates Reduction Act will have the effect of postponing for another 12 months this full increase of 17 per cent. In the meantime the government will have a chance to consider the recommendations contained in the first volume of the MacPherson commission report. We shall also be given the opportunity of waiting for the second and third volumes. The first volume contains some extremely important statements concerning matters affecting the railways that depended mostly on legislative action by various governments, our predecessors or ourselves. The second volume will deal mostly with regional aspects, regional anomalies and regional problems that affect the welfare of our railroads in Canada. That is why the government has decided to carry on for up to another 12 months this Freight Rates Reduction Act, and has also decided to vote another $20 million to take care of this difference between 8 per cent and 17 per cent.
This is a general outline of this resolution. When the bill is brought down hon. members will find that it contains provision to take care of the period between today and April 30 next. I know that hon. members opposite have asked what the government was going to do about the matter or what was going to happen in this period; whether the railways were going to be reimbursed for the amount of money they will lose because freight rates were not increased by the full 17 per cent. The bill will look after this matter, and will ensure that the railways and the shippers will not be taxed more than they would have been taxed if this present amendment had been brought in prior to April 30.
I therefore recommend to the committee that this resolution be adopted. It is my intention, after second reading of the bill, to move that it be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph


lines, as were the amendments to this bill last year and the year before. I therefore recommend the adoption of this resolution.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure the committee has listened with great interest to the statement the minister has made in connection with this resolution which is now before us. The resolution is a simple one. It concerns the extension of an act which was passed by this house on an earlier occasion, known as the Freight Rates Reduction Act. It can be divided into two parts; first, the extension of the act for a period of 12 months, and second, the increase in the subsidy to the total of $55 million over the three periods that the act has been in operation.
I would remind the minister that in his statement a moment ago he said the last time the act had been amended by his predecessor it was extended for a period of 12 months. My recollection is that the extension was for a period of nine and not 12 months. The minister has also said-and he will correct me if I am wrong-that the object of bringing in this resolution now is to give the government a breathing spell in order to allow them to consider the recommendations in the first volume of the report of the royal commission on transportation, together with the other two volumes which will be coming in due course.
If I am right in the inference which I obtained from what the minister said, I take it that there will be no legislation based on the report of the royal commission on transportation during the course of the present session. I say this because if the intention is to extend this act for a period of 12 months in order to give the government time to consider the recommendations of the royal commission, I take it there is not much hope of such legislation during the course of the present session of parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I just interject a word here. I do not want to mislead the committee. Actually I stated that this amendment will be for up to 12 months, but any time it were necessary to interrupt the provisions of this act, it could be done. I do not say it will last for 12 months, but it will be up to a maximum of 12 months.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I thank the minister for the statement he has made. The minister now indicates that while the extension is for 12 months, it may be interrupted during the course of that 12 month period by legislation which would be brought down to deal with the situation in accordance with the recommendations of the royal commission on transportation.

I must at the outset of my remarks deprecate the manner in which the government has dealt with this particular piece of legislation. The reason for that statement is that no intention was indicated by the government until the last days of the month of April. The prior act expired on April 30, and up until a day or two before that date there was no indication by the government to either the railways or the shippers of what the government intended to do in this situation. Therefore it was clear that the mind of the government either was not made up, or the government had entirely forgotten that the act was coming to an end on April 30, 1961. This is indicated not only from the questions asked in the house but also from information which anyone can obtain at the board of transport commissioners, because while the committee knows that the board of transport commissioners cannot make freight rates retroactive, the railways may, if they wish, file a tariff in reduction of rates.
The information I have in my possession is that the railways did file a tariff on or about April 28 which, because the government had not made up its mind, indicated as alternatives either (1) a tariff seeking to increase freight rates to the 17 per cent which was authorized on November 18, 1958, or (2) maintaining the freight rates at the level contained in the act of 1960, namely with the 8 per cent increase. Therefore I do not think there is any doubt that up until that time the government had not made up its mind what it intended to do.
That is indicative of the attitude of the government on this whole problem. I should like to put on record some of the statements made by the Prime Minister during the campaign of 1957. At Drumheller, Alberta, on May 18, 1957, in the Canadian Press report in the Montreal Gazette the Prime Minister is quoted as saying:
On freight rates, he said that a rate pattern discriminatory to the west has been made worse by recent increases. This had struck "an almost paralysing blow" to industrial development in the west.
And according to the Toronto Globe and Mail of May 20, 1957:
He said a Conservative government would equalize freight rates as far as possible to help both agriculture and industry on the prairies compete with the rest of Canada.
Then again during the campaign of 1958, according to a Canadian Press report in the Windsor Daily Star of February 14, 1958, the Prime Minister said:
On freight rates, Mr. Diefenbaker spelled out for the first time his government's apparent intention on the increase granted in January by the board of transport commissioners.
Freight Rates Reduction Act
I would ask the committee to pay particular attention to this passage:
"We said before we were in power that freight rates were unjustifiably high when raised horizontally. Did we act? When the board allowed an increase we held it up because it couldn't be justifiably brought into existence on the basis the increase was provided".
What happened after this statement was made was that an application was made by the railways of Canada to the board of transport commissioners to increase freight rates to the extent of 17 per cent. That application was granted by the board but there was an appeal to the cabinet by the provinces and others under the requisite section of the Railway Act and the appeal to the cabinet from that decision was granted.
Therefore, notwithstanding the words of the Prime Minister in his campaigning of 1958, the high freight rates about which he complained, and the horizontal increases, were worsened to the extent of 17 per cent.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext: I will deal with the roll back subsidy in a moment. I hope the Minister of Justice will enter this debate and tell us just how the statements made by both the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs, in his capacity as Acting Prime Minister, have been carried out. Incidentally, I have sent a note to the Prime Minister's office advising him that I intend to deal with this matter now.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext: Where is he?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext: Neither of those statements have been carried out by this government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit me to say that it is quite true he sent a note to the Prime Minister's office but I should tell him that it reached the Prime Minister's office almost coincidentally with my hon. friend's intervention in this debate, and after the Prime Minister was involved in another engagement which prevents him from being here at the present time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext:
I hope the Prime Minister will not enter this house on another occasion, as he has done before, and say that I have taken advantage of his absence to make a statement when he was not present. At any time the Prime Minister was not present he was, as the Minister of Justice has said, away on other important business-I am sure the Prime Minister cannot always be here-but he should not say that statements are made in this house in his absence with the implication that they are made intentionally then.
To carry on, if I may-I have only limited time-after that the cabinet decided to dismiss this appeal and allow the 17 per cent increase to go into effect, and the Secretary of State for External Affairs in his capacity as Acting Prime Minister made the following statement, which I should like to put on the record; and I draw this particularly to the attention of the Minister of Justice, who interrupted me a moment ago. The statement is dated November 26, 1958 and reads in part as follows:
The Honourable Howard Green, Acting Prime Minister, issued the following statement today on behalf of the government:
On the hearing of the appeal from the decision of the board of transport commissioners awarding the railways an increase in freight rates in order to meet a proposed increase in wages, it was agreed by the eight provinces and the railways
(1)	that the wage increases are reasonable
(2)	that a railway strike would be a national disaster and must be avoided.
They disagreed on the propriety of the action of the board of transport commissioners in basing an increase in freight rates on an anticipated wage increase which had not been unconditionally agreed upon by the railways and their employees; the provinces asked that the order made by the board be disallowed on this ground.
[The Chairman.]
We consider that, in future, the railways and their employees must come to a definite agreement before a wage increase should be accepted by the board of transport commissioners as the basis for an increase in freight rates, otherwise the board, as it foresaw itself, is apt to be forced into making Judgments about wage settlements which are not its proper responsibility. In the present case we are not allowing the appeal on this ground because to do so at this stage would precipitate a nation wide strike over an increase in wages as recommended by a conciliation board which increase neither the railways nor the provinces have resisted or will resist.
Then, Mr. Chairman, I draw the following words of the Acting Prime Minister to this committee:
The suggestion was made that these wage increases should be paid from the federal treasury. We do not intend to embark upon a policy of subsidizing wage increases; there would be no end to demands on all governments if such a policy were adopted.
What is this bill we are dealing with now, and what was the freight rate reduction bill of 1959-60, if not a subsidy?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext: This is not a subsidy in respect of wages.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext:
How do the words of the Acting Prime Minister compare with the legislation which is now before this committee and which was also then before the house? The statement continues as follows:
It is however recognized by the government that there are serious inequities in the present freight rate structure which have both contributed to, and been aggravated by, the system of horizontal rate increases. The government has already indicated its intention to move toward a solution of these problems.
It was only after that, namely May 13, 1959 -quite some time after-that the order in council establishing the royal commission on transportation was set up.
I should like to make two points clear in respect of that statement made by the Acting Prime Minister. The first point is, that exactly what he said the government should not do is being done in this legislation. The second point is-

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext: This has nothing to do with wages.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext: I am not talking about wages now, I am talking about subsidies.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext: You said before it was a wage subsidy, but it is not a wage subsidy.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext: When is a subsidy not a subsidy?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext: I did not say that at all. I quoted the words of the Acting Prime Minister, who said that.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext: You are all mixed up.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext:
Some hon. member on the other side suggests I am all mixed up, but I would suggest that the government has never been in such a chaotic state so far as freight rates are concerned as it is at the moment.
The Acting Prime Minister complained about the injustice and inequities in respect of horizontal rate increases. That statement was made three and a half to four years ago, and what has been done to do away with the inequities of horizontal freight rate increase? I suggest they have been worsened, first of all by the 17 per cent increase in freight rates, and then worsened again in connection with the extended 8 per cent change in respect of subsidies under the Freight Rates Reduction Act in 1959-60 and now again under this measure. So that the position, in so far as inequities of horizontal increases in freight rates are concerned, is much worse now in 1961 than it was when the Acting Prime Minister made his statement. There is no doubt that in respect of this act, as well as in respect of the whole field of freight rates, the government has certainly made a complete mess of it.
There are one or two other matters which I feel I should direct to the attention of the committee. The order in council setting up the commission, P.C. 1959-577 dated May 13, 1959 had, amongst others, the two following objectives to consider:
(a)	Inequities in the freight rates structure, their incidence upon the various regions of Canada and the legislative and other changes that can and should be made, in furtherance of national economic policy, to remove or alleviate such inequities;
(b)	The obligations and limitations imposed upon railways by law for reasons of public policy, and what can and should be done to ensure a more equitable distribution of any burden which may be found to result therefrom.
The first objective of the royal commission on transportation was to remove the inequities in the freight rate structure. Has anything been done in this respect? I ask the minister to indicate whether the government, since it came into office in 1957, has done anything to remove the inequities of the freight rate structure.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext: That is precisely why we set up the royal commission, to investigate this whole matter.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext:
That is not what the Prime Minister said. I placed his words on record the other day and I will do so again. When we were discussing the continuation of the work of the railway employees in November of last year the Prime Minister indicated quite clearly one of the reasons the royal commission was established. At page 359 of Hansard for November 30, 1960 the Prime Minister had the following to say:
Freight Rates Reduction Act
The reason we say we are waiting for the report of the royal commission is this. It will make its report as to the means whereby these discriminatory rates may be avoided.
Has it done that? I asked the question a moment ago. That is the reason this is being done. Well, the Prime Minister said:
It will make its report as to the means whereby these discriminatory rates may be avoided. Legislation will then be introduced in order to equalize opportunity across Canada. The freeze will then be taken off and the railway companies may then make an application to the board of transport commissioners to raise the freight rates and to take into consideration the agreements now in existence between the employers and the unions back to January 1, 1960.
Four things were set out by the Prime Minister. Not one of them has been accomplished. First, the inequities would be removed by the report of the royal commission. Next, freight rates would be equalized across the country. Third, the freeze would be lifted; and fourth, the railways could apply for increased freight rates.

In the case of the Canadian National Railways the taxpayers of this country are already being called upon to make up huge deficits. To require the Canadian taxpayer to subsidize the operating costs of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company would be setting a most dangerous and costly precedent.
Did the Minister of Labour make this statement?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES

What the minister says
simply confirms the argument that I am attempting to develop. A moment ago he said the government must have a breathing space in which to think this whole matter over, but that breathing space is certainly going to last more than a couple of months. This is a matter which the government cannot get away from. It is a matter on which parliament is entitled to have some information. It is a matter

on which absolutely no light has been thrown either by the Minister of Labour, the Minister of Transport or the Prime Minister himself. On the contrary, the statements they have made indicate quite clearly that there is going to be no policy of subsidization, although the measure now before us is subsidization for wages.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext:
I am worried about parliament. I think parliament is entitled to know. I think parliament should not be kept in the dark. I think the government should tell us, as the Prime Minister told us on November 30 what would be done; that legislation would be introduced to implement the recommendations of the royal commission, that the freight rate freeze would be lifted, and that the unions would be able to bargain with their employers, in accordance with the agreements. That is what he said. None of that is being done. It would have been much better if he had not said anything in that particular respect.
Then when he spoke on television the other night he said that the government was responsible for the settling of the strike. I do not know what the government did to settle the strike. It certainly did not take an active part in the settlement. In answer to a question which was put to him earlier, before the strike was settled, the Prime Minister made it quite clear that he had invited the parties to get together, and his reply was that the government had not been successful at that time in getting them together. That is what I am complaining about, if my hon. friend wants to know.
Before this debate is concluded I think we should get a clear indication from the minister and the government of what is going to happen. So far as the retroactive date of this legislation is concerned, I think any comment I have to make in that respect will have to await the bill. I believe it is advisable, as has been recommended, that this matter be referred to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines so that the trucking industry and the provinces, if they feel so disposed, can make recommendations in this respect.
I want to point particularly to two things. The first is the chaotic situation in which the transportation situation now is because of the indecision and hesitation of the government. The second is the fact that the
Freight Rates Reduction Act government did not realize that this particular act was coming to an end on April 30 of this year and took no steps to introduce this legislation until the dying days of the month of April, contrary to what was done on previous occasions when notice was given to shippers, the railways, the board of transport commissioners and the country as to what they could expect. After all, it is the board of transport commissioners that fixes the rates by order, and the board cannot make rates retroactive. As the Leader of the Opposition points out to me, it is contrary to the pledge on the part of the government. So I say that the government has failed on these two counts.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we support this resolution as we have on the two previous occasions when similar resolutions have been before us. We will vote for it, but this does not mean that our approval is not conditioned by the view that it is a palliative and an expedient on a very short range basis. I should like to emphasize the criticisms that have just been made which it seems to me are to this effect, that this is another example of the procrastination, posturing and indefiniteness of the government with respect to its policy in the field of transportation.
The hon. member for Laurier is sceptical about the past record of the government in relation to the railways. He pointed out that before the election in March, 1958, the government put a freeze on freight rates. As the hon. member for Assiniboia has said on former occasions, this was a brave act. But once the election was over and the railways came back with a further application the freeze disappeared and we had this subsidy. I think hon. members should be aware that the subsidy is extended to the Canadian National Railways, a publicly owned organization, and to the Canadian Pacific Railway, a private organization.
The whole idea of the subsidy was conceived in those dark months in the fall of 1958 when, according to rumours, the present Minister of Veterans Affairs led a revolt in the cabinet against the whole idea of freight rate increases. There have been press reports as to what occurred. As I remember, the Prime Minister was out of the country and the then minister of public works was in charge. There was quite a little battle over the matter, and this legislation was the solution.
Apparently $20 million was all that the western members of the cabinet were able to pry out of the Minister of Finance. It was recognized by all members who followed the legislation that the subsidy was not adequate to meet the increase and was only

Freight Rates Reduction Act a partial or half-way measure. The hon. member for Laurier has indicated by quotations from what the Prime Minister has said in the past that there have been many inconsistencies in his arguments. I hate to read from old records, but there is one paragraph in the announcement made by the former minister of transport when he first introduced this legislation which I think underlines the point made by the hon. member for Laurier. As found on page 2208 of Hansard of March 24, 1959 he said:
As hon. members know, the government has indicated its intention of proceeding with a comprehensive inquiry into matters affecting the railways. The proposed legislation therefore limits the assistance to a 12-month period, when it is hoped a report will be available to the government.
I point out that this was over two years ago. This is the capacity of foresight that the government seems to have. Over two years ago the minister predicted a report in about a year's time, and the report actually appeared another year later. In other words, it took two years instead of one and we now have only part of the report. At that time the minister went on to say:
Consideration will then be given-
That is, when the report is available.
-to means of further relieving the unfair discriminatory burden of the freight rates structure.
We do not know what the steps are going to be but it is quite apparent that we are not going. to get this legislation this session unless we work all through the summer and have a fall session. I have indicated previously that I feel we are on the eve of a general election. It seems to me that this kind of part-way measure is just a means of clearing the way for a general election without really revealing the government's policy. I should like the minister to tell us whether they feel it is possible for them to go ahead on the freight rates matter with only one volume of the MacPherson commission report. If it is not, when do they feel they can act to rationalize or equalize the whole freight rates question? One cannot help but be cynical or sceptical of their record in view of the way they have diddled and dawdled along with the transportation question.
The matter of the strike that was averted by the settlement between the railways and the unions a few weeks ago is another very good indicator of how the government has procrastinated with regard to the transportation problem. We were glad to see a settlement, but we are left with unanswered questions which it seems to me will be still floating around during a general election.


From the reaction of railway employees I know that the heat is off now and their sensitivity is sinking. It is much less keen that it was a month ago and, politically speaking, this is an ideal situation for the government in relation to an election.
However, the settlement does not really answer the problem that other speakers have brought up; where is the money coming from for the raise? It is not going to come from this legislation, because this is just a partial palliative; and since the railways have only signed a two year contract with the unions and since the contract runs out at the end of this year, we are going to be involved next year again in the same dreary round of conciliation boards, high cost reports and analyses and frustration on the part of everyone in relation to the railway problem.
I could point out to the minister, for example, that the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific got together and approached the Woods Gordon Company. This company turned out a rather extensive report, which I have read, which would supply the railways with a standard approach to entering into wage negotiations. The minister knows, if he has read the Milvain report, Judge Milvain really threw that extensive report right out the window. I hear now through the grapevine that the railways are right back with Woods Gordon again. They have assigned this organization to do another study in the same field. This is an example of the continual frustration and expense that is involved when you do not have a clear transportation pattern or picture presented to you by the government.
The general satisfaction that is felt in most parts of the country over the fact the royal commission report is now available must be tempered by the fact we have had no real indication from the government as to its response to these recommendations. The response of the country as a whole has been generally favourable, except perhaps in western Canada where there are still some very vivid criticisms of the recommendations in relation to the grain rates. Here again, as every member from the west knows, the Crowsnest pass rate is a fundamental political issue in western Canada. This is a bread and butter issue, and it seems to me that the government has moved itself into a situation where it has not answered the question of what is involved in the report on the Crowsnest pass rates. The government has not indicated what it is going to do about this recommendation. Consequently, the whole election in western Canada is going to be fought in a bit of a vacuum or will be surrounded by mystery.

I saw an excellent editorial in the Manitoba Co-Operator for April 29 of this year dealing with the transportation commission. The editorial stresses that the western farmer must take a new look at the recommendations, not only in relation to the subsidy for grain rates but also the matter of passenger service abandonment and branch line abandonment. The Co-Operator stressed the dissenting report of Mr. Gobeil and said it made very good sense to them. He raised a fundamental question about the Crowsnest pass rates which should be answered. The keynote here which I bring to the attention of the minister is that in western Canada the royal commission report has not removed the suspicions with which the people look at the Canadian Pacific Railway. I hope the minister has noted what the commissioners say about the Canadian Pacific Railway's case in connection with the grain issue. Certainly, the Canadian Pacific did not prove that they suffered a tremendous loss through the carriage of grain. I am sure western Canadian members will have some views to express on this question. I am not asking on their behalf but on behalf of this group for a statement from the minister regarding the government's position in so far as the commission's recommendations with regard to the Canadian Pacific Railway are concerned.
There is one question that I think troubles many members and has been troubling them for a long time. The Canadian Pacific Railway pension situation is not nearly as attractive or decent in relation to former employees as is that of the Canadian National Railways. On a previous occasion the Prime Minister indicated that our committee on railways was going to go into this whole pension matter. I imagine all members have received representations from the various organizations representing borth former Canadian National and Canadian Pacific employees. You might ask, Mr. Chairman, what relevance this has to this measure. Previously, we have had a very wide ranging debate on such measures, and I should like to suggest it is time we asked the government what it intends to do to bring the Canadian Pacific into line on this pension issue. It is worth while to ask this question because this measure we are discussing relates to a subsidy not only for the shippers but also for the Canadian Pacific Railway.
There is one other factor with which I wish the minister to deal at this time. The hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort has a bill on the order paper for the purpose of bringing rapeseed within the meaning of the term "grain", in order that it can gain the advantage of certain rates. Since I have been a member of the house, this issue has been
Freight Rates Reduction Act brought up every year by the representatives from that particular region. It seems to me that this is another part of the transportation picture to which we should have an answer at this stage. Why is it the government does not feel it can give this particular product the benefits of the subsidies that are now in existence in so far as freight rates are concerned? The debate on this measure, Mr. Chairman, will probably be a relatively short one. I ask the minister if, before it concludes, he could not give us some kind of projected schedule as to when we will get legislation that represents conclusions drawn from this MacPherson report. I should like him to be as frank and as candid as he possibly can because the whole matter of the wage increases that will be sought fairly soon, we can be sure, by the railway unions-perhaps toward the end of this year-will result again in a climate of dissent and disagreement, and a feeling of uneasiness will again be abroad in the country. This may be done after a general election has taken place, but it seems to me that an honest government would do its best to lay its cards on the table before we have an election.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext: Would you say this was not an honest government?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext:
I did not say that at all. I just said that I thought an honest government would lay its cards on the table before it went to the people on an issue as big as this which affects as much of the country as this does. We have been very much disturbed by this whole freight rate question. The region I represent, the bridge region, has been up in the air. This region made very strong representations to the MacPherson commission. We know that the prairie provinces spent thousands and thousands of dollars for counsel and presentations to the commission. British Columbia is vitally involved. Their member of this commission entered a dissenting report. We feel that in this kind of situation the honest government is the government that puts its cards on the table so that we know what it plans to do and when it plans to do it.
One aspect of this question was brought up by the hon. member for Laurier. He asked where the money is coming from to pay the wage increases. Is there going to be a later subsidy? As I indicated, this measure is only a palliative.
In reply to the hon. member for Cariboo, I would say that I would not go around labeling any government either honest or dishonest except in a specific situation. Surely, this is a specific situation that calls for honesty. All I can point out is that the transport minister, when he first introduced this legislation, was
4824	HOUSE OF
Freight Rates Reduction Act mistaken in his estimate as to how long it was going to take and what was going to flow from the government's policy. I think if the hon. member checks Hansard he will find this government said it expected to be able to act in one year. Instead, we have had one postponement and then another postponement. Here we are, over two years later, and we still are not in a position to know the policy or direction in which we are going. This is not an accusation of dishonesty, it is an accusation of procrastination and indecisiveness, of not being able to really plan the legislative future. I do not see how the hon. member could disagree with this analysis, even if he does support the government. If he wants to make the kind of contribution he can make perhaps more effectively in the caucus than here, I suggest that he along with other members keep pressing in caucus for the transportation policy of this government. I refer to the policy that it hopes to take to the people and not this short range palliative.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext:
I should like to say a few words while this resolution is being debated. Freight rates have an important bearing upon the cost of living and the conduct of business in Newfoundland and, in fact, in all the Atlantic provinces. We are a considerable distance away from the industrial centre of Canada. As I have pointed out previously, we in Newfoundland import practically everything we use, everything we wear and most of what we eat. Freight rates are therefore of vital importance to those of us who live in Newfoundland and in the Atlantic provinces; and any statements made with regard to freight rates or any legislation passed in relation thereto must command our intense interest. Our economy depends, to perhaps a greater extent than that of any other part of Canada, on the cost of moving goods.
I should like to call attention to an advertisement which must have been very appealing at the time it appeared because of the interest taken in this matter by the part of Canada from which I come. I refer to an advertisement which appeared in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of June 8, 1957. The advertisement was appropriately edged in black and blue and it urged maritimers to vote Progressive Conservative. It contained this pledge:
We are committed to the original pledge given to our people at the time of confederation that freight rates would be adjusted and transportation facilities would be provided so that our geographic position would not prejudice our producers in having reasonable access to the markets of Canada.
That was a noble sentiment and it no doubt affected advantageously the political fortunes of some hon. members. But what in fact happened? What happened was this, if I may


make a brief resume of subsequent events. The board of transport commissioners allowed or approved an increase of 17 per cent. In 1959, parliament cut this figure down to 10 per cent and later, in the next year, cut it to 8 per cent, paying the difference between that figure and 17 per cent. I suppose the idea now, if my understanding of it is correct, is that parliament will approve the payment of the difference to the railways so that they will still get 17 per cent in order to meet their wage bills.
Be that as it may, the cost of transportation is still up and it bears very heavily on a section of Canada which is least able to pay high costs. By virtue of our geographic position on the eastern seaboard there is a longer haul to get vital supplies in, the goods manufactured in central Canada, the things that are used in normal daily existence, as I mentioned previously, such as food, clothing and so on. These things have to be brought in to Newfoundland from various parts of Canada. They have to be loaded at the port of North Sydney, unloaded at Port aux Basques and loaded on railway cars or perhaps loaded on ships for various ports and unloaded again. Any way you look at it, the cost of transportation is bound to be high unless effect is given to this principle which appears in the advertisement I mentioned and which reads:
-freight rates would be adjusted and transportation facilities would be provided so that our geographic position would not prejudice our producers-
And so on. It would appear from the record that this has not been done and that the Atlantic provinces still suffer from freight rates which are too high and which bear unequally on a part of Canada which provides an important market for the rest of Canada.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext: How did that situation occur?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext: I beg the hon. member's pardon? How did what situation occur?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext: How did discrimination in freight rates occur?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext:
All I have to say in answer to that question is this. The discrimination has not been removed in accordance with the pledge of the party of the hon. member; and the fact is that a part of Canada which is important economically to the rest of Canada has its own purchasing power reduced and its economic expansion curtailed because of a freight rate scale which is too high. I would ask the minister to keep this matter in mind and to remember that there is real advantage in a policy such as this, to quote again from the pledge:

-that freight rates would be adjusted and transportation facilities would be provided so that our geographic position would not prejudice our producers in having reasonable access to the markets of Canada.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext:
I do not wish to prolong this discussion as there will be an opportunity to speak again when the bill founded on this resolution is introduced. At that time we shall be able to make our position known with regard to the details of the legislation which is now contemplated. However, in view of the minister's introduction of this resolution and the importance of the principle involved in it, I wish to say something at this time.
In the first place I should like to reiterate and emphasize what my friend the hon. member for Laurier said a few moments ago, namely that when the Prime Minister and the present government took office in 1957 they were pledged to the elimination of horizontal freight rate increases. There can be no doubt about that pledge. At that time the Prime Minister made it perfectly clear that he would stop all these inequitable freight rate increases and would bring in an alternative policy which would be far more effective in dealing with the problem than the device of horizontal increases.
We soon learned what this pledge meant. The threat of the strike in 1958 made that matter perfectly clear; the fact that there would be no such long range policy introduced. On November 27, 1958, the government provided for a horizontal increase of 17 per cent with a view no doubt to preventing the strike. Our position as a party at that time was made perfectly clear in a statement then released and I do not wish to repeat it now. It may be necessary to put it on the record later. This increase was compensated, in part, by legislation reaffirming and introducing again the principle of subsidies, which brought down the impact of the increase by, I think it was 9 per cent. But it left the principle itself intact.
That legislation has been renewed. We are now being asked to renew it again. As my hon. friend from Port Arthur pointed out, this is itself proof that the government in the years since has had no long range policy to put before the house in respect of this important matter.
Of course, the minister will say, "Oh, well, we set up a royal commission to deal with this matter", and the recommendations of this royal commission will no doubt in due course be implemented. I think we were told in the house the other day that it is the intention of the government to implement them in part-at least in part.
However, it is quite clear that whatever may be the intentions of the government 90205-6-305
Freight Rates Reduction Act with regard to the recommendations of this particular royal commission, those intentions cannot be carried out to deal with the present situation in which the railways now find themselves, having a few days ago accepted the recommendations of the conciliation board in regard to wage increases.
We have been asking the minister how the railways are going to meet this new obligation which they told us through the government last November and December they could not possibly meet, that they were not in a position to meet. The minister says, "Oh, these recommendations will in due course put the railways on their feet. They will make possible improvements in railway management. Operations will be more economical and they will be able to get out of some uneconomic activities. As a result of this they will be in a better position to raise wages to the level which is demanded".
But this is not going to help the railways meet this particular demand which they have accepted. As a result of their acceptance a strike was prevented in May on exactly the same basis as we suggested last November it should be prevented. Therefore we ask the minister, when he winds up this discussion, to tell us how the railways are going to do now, in respect of this matter, something they found it quite impossible to do last December.
Last November and December when this matter was being debated, spokesmen for the government, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Labour, made it quite clear that the attitude would be that taken by the Acting Prime Minister, in 1958 I think it was; that subsidies would not be resorted to as a way out of these difficulties. This was still going to be the decision of the government-no subsidies. We need not put anything more on the record on that score.
The minister now says, "Subsidies specifically tied in to wage increases are one thing, but subsidies for something else as recommended in a royal commission report are different". But a subsidy used by the railway for one purpose can help that same railway in some other respect; in connection with wage increases or anything else, because it is quite clear that if you help the railway in one direction you will help it in another.
The government's position is that the railways should not be assisted through subsidy but that wage increases-and I want to be fair to the minister in this-should be made possible, when desirable, by the removal of discriminatory freight rates. That was the position taken, we know, by the government in November and December. But having taken that position, the Prime Minister said this would be done through the royal commission

Freight Rates Reduction Act in time to be effective before the strike deadline of May 15. There can be no doubt about that, and there is no use of the minister or anybody else trying to tell the committee that what the Prime Minister had in mind was that ultimately these things would be corrected, discriminations would be removed and everything would be all right in the future.
I say this because the Prime Minister's words are so clear that there can be no reason for any misunderstanding. I am going to read them. At page 359 of Hansard of November 30, 1960, the Prime Minister is reported as having said:
The reason we say we are waiting for the report of the royal commission is this. It will make its report as to the means whereby these discriminatory rates may he avoided. Legislation will then be introduced in order to equalize opportunity across Canada.
All this would be done to avoid a railway strike. Then the Prime Minister went on:
The companies may then make an application to the hoard of transport commissioners to raise the freight rates and to take into consideration the agreements now in existence between the employers and the unions back to January 1, 1960.
If that were not clear enough, the Prime Minister repeated it on December 1 at page 370 of Hansard. This time he put the date in at which these things would be done, he said, "By next May 15-". Not May 15, 1962, 1963 or whenever the royal commission will have completed all its work, but he said:
By next May 15, without the sacrifice of anything except a postponement, every railway employee will be in a position through his bargaining agent to come to an agreement with the railway company. The railway company will be able to apply to the board of transport commissioners. The freeze will be lifted and the Canadian people, in the normal run of events, will then have to pay extra freight rates in order to meet the increased wage levels, just as they have to pay to meet all other types and varieties of expenditure.
So I ask the minister, when he replies, to tell us whether this is the situation now? Of course it is not; it has not been so. The strike was prevented, but not on the basis stated by the Prime Minister in those two excerpts from Hansard which I have just read. There can be no doubt about that.
Something else has happened. A great mystery has developed as to how this was done, and perhaps the minister will enlighten us in due course as to that mystery and what has been done to make it possible for the railways to do in May what they said they could not do in December. Perhaps the government is going to put a $1 item in the supplementary estimates which will make it easier.
There is something else which certainly should be brought to the attention of this committee. I regret doing this while the


Prime Minister is not here, because it is a report in the press which refers directly to a statement made by the Prime Minister. However, it is a statement to which a good deal of attention has been given and which has not been corrected, so far as I know.
It deals with the resolution which was put on the order paper-the resolution which we are now discussing-and more particularly in regard to the retroactivity of the legislation which was required because of the carelessness of the government in not bringing in this legislation before April 30.
There is a Canadian Press story about this dated April 25 and I quote from it:
Prime Minister Diefenbaker said Friday-
This was not in the house, but outside, I believe:
-legislation to extend the $20 million a year rollback subsidy on freight rates will be made retroactive to May 1 when it is passed by parliament.
It is obvious that this has to be done because it was not brought in when it should have been. Then the story goes on:
Present legislation authorizing the subsidy, under which the federal treasury has put up $35 million in the last 21 months to counteract a 17 per cent freight rate increase granted in 1958, expires Sunday night.
That is the $35 million to take the place of this long range policy that the Prime Minister was going to introduce in 1957. Then the story goes on, and this is the important and astonishing part of it. It is almost impossible to believe that this is accurate. Here it is, however:
Mr. Diefenbaker was asked whether it would be necessary for parb'ament to act on the extension today in order to assure there is no lapse.
He said the government notice given the commons earlier this week would act in the same way as a budget proposal which becomes effective when it is announced, subject to later parliamentary approval.
I should be glad to hear the minister answer that statement which is attributed to the Prime Minister and not changed or corrected since that time; which lays down the incredible doctrine that legislation of this kind, which is to be made retroactive, because it is the same as a budget resolution, becomes automatically retroactive, when it is passed, to the date the resolution was put on the order paper. This is something entirely new to constitutional law and parliamentary practice. To give the impression, through a story of that kind in the Canadian press, that whether we bring this legislation in after April 30 or not, when the legislation is passed it becomes retroactive in the same form as a budget resolution, to the date of its introduction, is, to use the politest words I can find,

misleading to anyone who reads the story. I would be very glad indeed to have the minister deal with this particular aspect of this particular resolution.
As I have said, Mr. Chairman, when the resolution is passed and the legislation is before the house, we will all have an opportunity to give it the kind of examination it deserves. Meanwhile, we have the right and duty at this time to express our disappointment, in and condemnation of, the government for, in May, 1961, introducing legislation to carry on for another year, or whatever term it may be, a policy which the government itself said in 1957 was wrong and would be changed if it were given the opportunity to make the change.
