I have one other matter to bring to the attention of the committee, Mr. Chairman, and on which to express my opinion. I refer to the responsibility of the railways so far as the general public is concerned. What I have in mind is the reduction of passenger service on the Kettle valley railway by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to which reduction people in my constituency and in east Kootenay as well object very much. I cannot see why those people are denied this opportunity. They are not asking for very much. They are simply asking for daily service with the present Budd car plus a combination cafe and sleeping car so that persons who wish to take a berth or a bedroom when going to the coast or returning would have that opportunity and an opportunity to sleep in a decent and civilized manner.
I cannot see why the railroad divorces its freight earnings from its passenger earnings. That section of the railroad is very profitable to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and yet they insist on this reduction of passenger service on the excuse that it does not pay. Perhaps the passenger service does not pay but the freight service certainly does and the people of my constituency, including chambers of commerce, trade unions, farm organizations and other people believe that the earnings of the railway, both freight and passenger, should be considered in the interests of the communities. In addition to that, the most profitable investment the Canadian Pacific Railway Company ever made, the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, is in this area. This is where it makes a considerable portion of its profits and yet the railroad insists on divorcing its railroad activities from its .other activities. We are of the opinion they should all be considered together. Whatever the opinion may be in that respect, the people I represent, and I am speaking very largely for the population, believe that, in view of the freight earnings in the district, in view of the interest of the Canadian Pacific in the district, there should be at least a daily service from Vancouver to Lethbridge over the Kettle valley and a combination cafe and sleeping car attached to the present Budd car. This is not asking very much when one considers the wealth that is produced in that area and the profits that go to the Canadian Pacific as a result of industrial activity in that area.
In the present circumstances we believe that the company is not accepting its responsibilities to the area concerned. In view of the fact that this government under this legislation and other legislation, and indirectly the people of Canada, are subsidizing this and other operations of this company,

we do urge that the government do everything possible to see that this situation is remedied.

Mr. Chairman, my purpose in rising to participate in this debate is to try to strike a blow for northwestern Ontario in its fight against freight rate discrimination. I cannot help but sound a note of disappointment at the government's failure to introduce this legislation sooner. We are led to believe that we are now on the last lap of this session, and if we are to end it around the end of June, then not much time remains to give proper consideration to matters of such great importance as our railways and freight rates.
The level of the freight rate structure brought about by the successive increases implemented during the post-war years has commanded increasing attention during the past year. The Freight Rates Reduction Act provided for a subsidy not exceeding $20 million for one year only, to reduce the burden of the 17 per cent increase in freight rates which the board authorized to become effective on December 1, 1958. On July 10, 1959, the board issued a further order substituting an increase of 10 per cent for the 17 per cent and directed that the adjusted rates be not increased for one year unless otherwise permitted by the board. At the time the legislation was passed the Prime Minister announced the appointment of a royal commission on transportation and the Minister of Transport stated that the government would not permit any further general increase in freight rates for an indefinite period, ostensibly pending the report of the royal commission.
I would imagine that the royal commission on transportation report of 92 pages has been and is being scrutinized by the government. It is an important report and one which requires many hours of close study because the recommendations contained therein are of such a nature that they could easily affect every facet of our economy. The report comprises 92 pages of technical data, and it includes also a minority report, mostly concerned with details of the Crowsnest rates on exports of grain. These Crowsnest rates are one of the biggest items within which a substantial area of disagreement may be found.
I am not at all sure that the continuation of these abnormally low rates, in the light of present day costs which are conservatively 10 times higher than they were when these rates were set, are justified. However, Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to develop an argument against them at this time. All I say is that this feature should be a matter deserving deep study.
There is the problem of regional freight rates, and the regional freight rates structures
Freight Rates Reduction Act with respect to which some sections of the country, such as northwestern Ontario as an example, have borne the brunt of discrimination for years. This should be one of the first matters to be considered when freight rates adjustments are made. I think it should be one of the duties of the government to bring forth a recommendation which will end such rank discrimination once and for all.
At page 29 of the report there is reference to the limitation of regulations consistent with public interest and fair treatment in all ways to all carriers.
At page 71 of the same report there is a statement on increases of rates to the effect that no one can or should guarantee that the revenue of any competitive business will be adequate. This is just as true of competitive transportation as of any other business.
Incidentally, the predecessor of the present Minister of Transport as reported at page 2208 of Hansard of 1959 had this to say in answer to a question:
Consideration will then be given to means of further relieving the unfair discriminatory burden of the freight rate structure. In the meantime the government does not propose to permit any further general increase in railway freight rates.
In that statement he definitely said that discrimination would be done away with and that a new era would come upon us so far as railway freight rates are concerned. The royal commission report has now been in the hands of the government for several months and we are awaiting the results of its study.

I accept the minister's correction. If he says it is only several weeks I will accept his statement. I was under the

Freight Rates Reduction Act impression it was longer. However, I may be wrong. In any event, we are now waiting lor the results, what the government will recommend and what it will not. In the meantime, and ever since the appointment of the commission over a year ago, freight rates have been in a freeze.
On numerous occasions, and more recently when the case of northwestern Ontario for more equitable rates based on common sense was presented to the royal commission sitting in the court house of the city of Port Arthur, we have pointed out that increases amounting to 157 per cent have been awarded the railways during the past 11 years and the result in high cost of freight has meant the loss of business and the discouragement of business in this area of Ontario. For the benefit of those who wonder why one section of Ontario protests high freight rates that are accepted in another section of the province of Ontario, the reason is that southern Ontario does not have to pay for the long haul around the great lakes. In this respect northwestern Ontario's position is more comparable with that of the prairie provinces where virtually all freight is long haul business.
Mr. Neil Edmenstone, vice president of Steep Rock iron mines, speaking before a chamber of commerce meeting at Fort William on March 22, 1961, had this to say:
We need freight rates that make economic sense to this area which will permit us to thrive and compete while permitting the railways to do the same. If the railways won't do it, then the government must act to do it. There are policies being mooted which would stop dead in its tracks the biggest development northwestern Ontario has ever had or may have for a long time to come.
The Prime Minister, speaking at Fredericton last December, made the statement that the government was against the railroads meeting union wage demands by increasing freight rates, and he went on to say:
We acted in the continuation of the operations of the railways without unfairness or injustice. Additional time was provided by the government's action to enable the royal commission to bring about equalization of opportunity everywhere in Canada.
Further on he added this significant statement:
To have allowed the railways to increase freight rates on a horizontal basis would have been to increase discrimination rates that now exist which deny the Atlantic provinces the possibility of expansion.
That is precisely the problem of northwestern Ontario. The situation there parallels that of the maritimes. I wish to cite several examples to show how this discrimination works to the detriment not only of the manufacturers but also the consumers. On a 30,000-pound car of canned foods from Chatham,
iMr. Badanai.]
Ontario, winter freight rates are as follows and, incidentally, they do not include heating charges: Chatham to Marathon or Geraldton, a distance of 783 miles, $1.57 per 100 pounds. The distance from Chatham to Fort William or Porth Arthur is 981 miles and the rate is $1.57 per 100 pounds. From Chatham to Atikokan, Ontario, the distance is 1,056 miles and the rate is $1.90 per 100 pounds. From Chatham to Winnipeg the distance is 1,400 miles and the rate is $1.65 per 100 pounds. You will notice the difference there. From Chatham to Atikokan the charge is $1.90 per 100 pounds for a distance of 1,056 miles and from Chatham to Winnipeg, a distance of 1,400 miles, or 344 miles farther, the rate is $1.65, which is much lower on a longer haul.
From Chatham to Regina, a distance of 1,756 miles, the rate is $3.01 per 100 pounds. From Chatham to Vancouver, a distance of 2,864 miles, the rate is $1.80 per 100 pounds. In other words, it costs less to send 100 pounds of canned goods from Chatham, Ontario, to Vancouver than it does to send 100 pounds of the same canned goods from Chatham to Atikokan although the mileage in the latter case is only a little more than one third.
If cars of canned goods roll to the lakehead for distribution and are hauled back to Geraldton or Marathon there is a further charge of $1.37 per 100 pounds for this 200-mile haul. This means that it actually costs 85 cents to freight one case of 24-15 ounce tins weighing 29 pounds from the canning plant to Marathon or Geraldton and this 85 cents represents a further cost of 32 per cent.
To take another example, one case of corn containing 24-15 ounce tins and costing $2.60 f.o.b. factory would cost $3.45 per case f.o.b. Geraldton or Marathon. Whereas a retailer will sell this corn in Chatham to the consuming public at two tins for 27 cents his counterpart in Marathon or Geraldton 783 miles away would of necessity have to sell it at two tins for 35 cents. These examples, and I could cite others, will suffice to indicate the discrepancies in these rates. These examples only show the vicious impact on the cost of living in northwestern Ontario which by no stretch of the imagination can be condoned any longer. The freight rate on a basic commodity such as wheat, which is subject to world market competition, could not be related in any way to the domestic market. Internal freight rates agreements should be made to enable the transportation companies to assess their rightful tariff, and then every section of Canada will carry its proper share of the load. The establishment of a fair freight rate structure for northwestern Ontario in general, and the lakehead area in

particular, is the key to the development and prosperity of this often forgotten but very important section of the province of Ontario.
This committee will recall, Mr. Chairman, the removal to Montreal of the passenger bus manufacturing facilities from the Canadian Car plant at Fort William. This was not caused by competition from General Motors, as was suggested by the hon. member for Port Arthur a few weeks ago but rather came about because of freight rate inequalities. We do not yet have the advantage of numerous adequate highways which would allow many of our important industries to obtain competitive rates. In addition, there are not too many examples of agreed rates in this territory. Horizontal freight rate increases have a harsher effect upon northwestern Ontario than is generally the case in many other parts of Canada. These conditions have meant that our small businesses, forced to use class rates extensively, bear an increasingly large percentage of the burden. Our people also bear this burden because everyone, directly or indirectly, pays freight rates which often amount to more annually than one's tax bill. We know two things about our present economy. It is distinguished by higher than average costs and higher than average unemployment. Each of these aspects is related, and both are related to high freight costs.
The rate structure as a whole is very sensitive to changes, and often a seemingly realistic adjustment can boomerang in the most unexpected place and manner. For example, the removal of the mountain differential looked good to British Columbia. However, it resulted in the cancellation of some reasonable commodity rates on British Columbia lumber to the Canadian lakehead, and raised that rate by 19 cents per 100 pounds. This was the start of conditions about which our industry has complained so bitterly. Our lumber and wood operators believe they can prove that the present rate structure is out of line with the development of their businesses and the development of the community.
The lakehead cities of Fort William and Port Arthur are situated in what has come to be called northwestern Ontario. In terms of railway mileage, these cities are 419 miles from Winnipeg, 551 miles from Sudbury and 810 miles from Toronto. This huge region, over 225,000 square miles in area, is crossed by the transcontinental line of Canadian National in its north centre, by the Canadian Pacific in its south centre, and by a line of Canadian National along its southern edge west of the lakehead. In freight rate terms, the western region begins at Fort William and at Armstrong to the north on the Canadian
Freight Rates Reduction Act National. Traditionally the lakehead cities have been the gateway to the west. Aside from this transportation aspect of our economy, the region's main industries and activities centre on the forests and the mines. The products are largely pulpwood, lumber, plywood, paper and poles, iron ore and base metals. Northwestern Ontario's case relating to freight rates stems from the effects of horizontal increases since 1948. These increases, as I have already pointed out, have amounted to 157 per cent. The cumulative effect of these increases has worked to the marked disadvantage of our territory where long distances make for high freight costs, inordinately increased by the percentage basis.
We are submitting to the government the importance of adjustments in these rates. As I have pointed out, this region has been more or less neglected for the past several years. I trust that the minister will have some answers to these questions when he sums up at the end of this debate, and that he will give some thought to the case of northwestern Ontario, a region which I am representing here at least in part because my own constituency is largely dependent upon industries which are seriously affected by freight rates.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to repeat the points that have already been made by the hon. member for Laurier and the Leader of the Opposition. I do intend, in somewhat different language and for the sake of emphasis, to repeat a point that was made by the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador.
First, I want to say something directly about the measure that is before us in view of the interjections that were made by the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Transport earlier this afternoon. The government did not see fit to bring the measure before parliament before it came into effect. These ministers say that what we are being asked to vote now, this $20 million for the year beginning May 1, is not a subsidy to support wages. This, of course, is just a fiction. Everybody knows that the 17 per cent freight rate increase was made in 1958 to meet the increase in wages. Everybody knows that the government allowed the 17 per cent increase to come into effect, and then decided that the shippers would pay part of it and the taxpayers would pay the rest of it. This is what happened. If one calls that a subsidy for some purpose other than for wages, one is just playing with words. It is true it is not a direct subsidy for wages but it is subsidy which is paid because wages went up. In consequence of wages going up, the board of transport commissioners allowed freight rates to

Freight Rates Reduction Act go up horizontally, notwithstanding the fact the Prime Minister promised in 1957 that we would have no more horizontal increases if the people voted for him. This was just another of those promises about which we have heard so much, but not recently, and about which hon. gentlemen opposite hate to be reminded.
The fact of the matter is that we should call a spade a spade. The government should not pretend things are not what they are because the government is not fooling anybody. This $20 million is a straight subsidy resulting from a freight rate increase which resulted from a wage increase. In other words, it is a subsidy for a wage increase. Why it was all right to provide a subsidy in respect of this matter, and why it became suddenly so wicked last November and December, it is rather difficult for people whose minds move reasonably logically to understand.
Having said that, Mr. Chairman, may I say that I think we also ought to remember that this legislation has been brought in because of another promise which was made by the Prime Minister and which he was unable or unwilling to keep. As the Leader of the Opposition pointed out following the hon. member for Laurier, the Prime Minister last November promised that a solution of this problem would be found; he promised that there would be no wage subsidy and that a solution would be found by the Mac-Pherson commission which would enable the railway labour dispute which could not be settled last December, to be settled before May 15. The Prime Minister also promised that he would bring in legislation to create conditions that would make that settlement possible. There has been no legislation. There has been no change whatsoever from the situation with which we were faced last November and December.

I am not making insulting innuendos at all. I am putting on the record what has been said about this matter. On May 5, as found at page 4401 of Hansard, I asked the Prime Minister this question:
Could I ask the Prime Minister to give an assurance that no prior undertaking of any description was given to the railway company before the settlement was reached yesterday?
Here is the Prime Minister's reply given in that courteous manner which so endears him to the house and to the country:

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext:
I say with the greatest joviality to the hon. gentleman that the experiences he used to have when he was a member of the government of a former day are not being repeated by this government.
I can tell you the experiences I had with Mr. St. Laurent. Mr. St. Laurent did not use double talk like that. When you asked Mr. St. Laurent a question, he gave a courteous and straightforward answer to it and he did not reflect on his predecessors who were no longer

in the house. The plain fact is that if Mr. St. Laurent had been asked a question like that in this house he would have said yes or no. We can only assume that the reason the Prime Minister did not say yes or no was that he was not willing to tell us what the arrangement was and yet he did not want to say there was no arrangement as there is an arrangement. That is the only inference one can draw from this kind of answer. Then I went on to ask this question:
I wonder if the Prime Minister could not now give a categorical answer to a simple, straightforward question.
Once more there was the usual courteous reply by the Prime Minister: silence.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES

Since the minister is asking the question, may I say this. In my view, if there were no such assurance the Prime Minister would say simply and in a straightforward manner, "There was no such assurance". Because he obviously evaded the question and because the railways have said they cannot find the money themselves, I think we are entitled to assume that they had such an assurance, either expressed or implied. If there is any respect for parliament in this government which professes to have so much respect for it, I think parliament should be told what that assurance was.
Parliament was told by the Prime Minister in the most categorical fashion last November and December that the royal commission was going to provide a solution to this problem. To my simple way of looking at it, the royal commission has provided no solution to this problem. If it has done so, will the government please tell us now what that solution is? Earlier, in reply to my hon. friend from Laurier, the Minister of Transport said that the subsidies which have been recommended by Mr. MacPherson's commission were not for the purpose of subsidizing wages. That is quite true. But if the government should, in its wisdom, some time before the end of this session bring in legislation or an item in the estimates in order to provide some of these subsidies, there is nothing to prevent the railways from using them, not for the purpose Mr. MacPherson recommended but, as my hon. friend from Laurier said, in order to meet this deficiency in revenue 90205-6-306
Freight Rates Reduction Act because of the increased wage rates. But at least parliament ought to be told what we are being asked to do and why we are being asked to do it.
If the government are going to bring in legislation to give a further subsidy to the railways, why could it not have been done today? Why could it not have been brought in with this measure instead of bringing two measures before the house? Why could we not have dealt with the whole problem at once? Is it because the government, as usual, do not know what on earth to do about the problem or is it because they wish to wait until the last day of the session, as they have done with many another controversial thing in every session since 1958, in the hope that they can get it through without much scrutiny and without much debate? I say, Mr. Chairman, that to bring in this stopgap measure that was brought in in 1959 and again last year-a stopgap measure that was to last only until the MacPherson commission had made its report-and now to bring it in again, and at the same time to refuse to tell the house and the country what their plans are is conduct that I do not understand. If the government have no respect for the house, surely they have some respect for the country. Surely we are entitled to know, as the representatives of the people, what the government's plans are for dealing with this urgent, grave and difficult problem.
I want to say a word, and just a word, about the measure as it affects another promise made by this government, the promise my hon. friend from Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador read to the committee earlier. Of course, this was in that high noon of promises in May of 1957. These are the promises that hon. gentlemen opposite would like to forget; they hate to have them mentioned.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I had not intended to make any remarks on this particular item because I think my views as to subsidizing the railroads are well known. The hon. member says it does not matter how you disguise it; it does not matter what you want to do for the railroads in the form of a subsidy, it is entirely the fault of the railroad employees and nobody else. It does not make any difference that they might have been operating passenger services that are uneconomical; it does not make any difference that they might be hauling grain below what it costs them to do it; it does not make any difference that they might be forced to operate uneconomical branch lines; the hon. member says that if a penny is paid to the railroads it is the fault of labour and nobody else. He says that every ill of the railroads is the fault of the employees.
I am absolutely surprised to hear a statement like that, not only from the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate but it has been implied all the way through by his colleague, the hon. member for Laurier, only the hon. member got up and put it a little more clearly than he did. If this government had taken the course of compulsory arbitration suggested by the Liberal party I am sure it would have taken away for all time the rights of the employees on the railroads to strike. We must remember that when the Liberal party was in power in 1950 this was their solution to the thing, to propose compulsory arbitration notwithstanding the fact that labour was entirely opposed to it.
Had the present government taken that course suggested by the opposition, compulsory arbitration would have been established for any dispute on the railways. There can be no doubt that had that happened there would have been the same suggestion on the part of the Liberal party to impose compulsory arbitration when any other serious labour dispute came about.
I am not going to deal any further with this particular subsidy except to say that I am concerned about it being continued again. I pointed out to the house when it was first instituted that subsides are very difficult to discontinue once they are started. This is now the third time that we are dealing with this particular question. I think the concern I had at that time has been shown to be not unfounded.
However, I realize the position the government is in through having just received the report of the royal commission on transportation, and having received only the first volume of that report. It was suggested by one hon. member of the opposition that the government has had this report for months and had done nothing about it. When we consider the actions of hon. members of the Liberal party when they were in office, they show a great deal more concern now for the passage of time than they did at that time. Freight Rates Reduction Act

Yes, and you made a big thing of it. I should just like to present certain figures, at this time, which I am not pulling out of a hat, in respect of those figures quoted this afternoon. I suggest by looking at the varying proportions regarding freight rate increases we will then have a clearer picture in respect of which government is more concerned with the welfare of Canadian citizens as far as freight rates are concerned.
Since 1945 freight rates have increased by 157 per cent. One hundred and forty per cent of this increase occurred during the time my hon. friend was a minister under the Liberal regime. During the Conservative administration-that is during the last four years-the only increase which has been allowed was to the extent of 10 per cent, which was later reduced to 8 per cent. In other words, the total increase of 17J per cent was originally decreased to 10 per cent, and then to 8 per cent. The government has also frozen all increases; this policy is still in effect. I suggest that this government has shown the people of Canada what it thought of the great burden of freight rates in various parts of the country. This government has looked into the matter seriously and has gone out of its way in an attempt to help the shippers of various regions of Canada, who have had to face these freight rate increases.

The hon. member for Laurier made a great fuss this afternoon about the fact that this amendment was being brought forward after April 30, and that the house was taken by surprise. He seemed to be suggesting that there was some kind of plot involved. I should like to remind the committee that the hon. member asked me a question, and I am sure he remembers it very well, prior to April 30, to which I replied that legislation was to be brought in to take care of the few days existing between April 30 and the time approval was given to this bill. I remember also being asked what was to happen in respect of the new rate which was filed by the railways, and I told the house that both railway presidents had written to me stating that these freight rates would not be applied. I would suggest, therefore, that not one single Canadian will have suffered any harm, in any way, shape or form as a result of this legislation being brought in at the present time. I should also suggest that the resolution was placed on the order paper before April 30, so no one was taken by surprise.
We wanted to act in a fashion which would permit both labour and management complete freedom to discuss these problems in an attempt to settle them in a manner that would be in accordance with the collective bargaining traditions of this government. We were very pleased to find that we did not have to impose any compulsory arbitration measures on one side or the other, because management and labour had come to an agreement. It has been suggested here this afternoon that the official opposition was disappointed because of that sudden settlement, however, I must say that we on this side quite freely admit that we are extremely pleased, and suggest that the rest of the people of Canada are extremely pleased, that the strike did not take place.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES

We have also this afternoon heard many expressions of criticism of the fact that the first report of the royal commission on transportation has been tabled now for one or two weeks, and that the government has as yet not introduced any legislation to implement the recommendations contained in that report. I suggest that my hon. friends opposite know very well that recommendations contained in reports of royal commissions are not dealt with in a matter of two or three days. This report is an extremely important one to be followed and complemented by two further volumes. Having read the first volume I feel that volume II will have a great impact on transportation in Canada.

Earlier in the afternoon, the hon. members for Fort William and Bonavista-Twillingate, as well as some others, referred to the problems which face the shippers in various regions of this country. As indicated by volume I of the MacPherson report, volume II will deal with the burden of freight rates on a comparison basis, as they affect different sections of the country. It is also the intention of the commission to include in volume II of its report recommendations concerning special transportation problems. I think it will be extremely important to see the two further volumes of the report of the royal commission on transportation.
My friend the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, in his unique fashion, this afternoon tried to build up a great plot on the part of the Prime Minister in his dealings with the railways' presidents. Maybe that is what happened a few years ago, but that is not the way things are done now. What happened is that the management of the railways and labour got together and discussed their problem, after the first volume of the royal commission report on transportation had been tabled. I remember the Prime Minister stating in November that the report of the royal commission on transportation would have quite a bearing on any discussion between the railways and labour. Of course, I am convinced that the report must have had quite a bearing on their discussion. We could tell by the opinions expressed both by Mr. Crump and Mr. Gordon, when the first volume of the report was published, that they were impressed by the first volume of the report. They expressed their satisfaction with many aspects of the report, and I am quite sure that it must have been one of the big factors in the railways deciding to meet the majority recommendation of the Milvain report. Of course, it was a decision taken freely by the presidents, by Mr. Hall and by the other labour leaders who signed the settlement agreement on behalf of the two parties.

Freight Rates Reduction Act The Prime Minister promised that his government would do something about this and that is why we appointed the royal commission to deal precisely with those injustices and anomalies and to make sure that Canadians from one end of the country to the other would be receiving the same treatment as far as freight rates and railway transportation are concerned.
The royal commission has produced its first report and the government of course is considering the first volume. It contains extremely interesting recommendations concerning aspects of the railway problem and the government is of course giving considerable study to the first volume of the report.
Since the report has been tabled the Prime Minister, in answering questions raised by my hon. friends, has said that we can expect interim legislation to be brought forward which will be based on certain parts of the MacPherson report. The government will certainly take into consideration the study made by the commissioners and of the principle expressed by them but, of course, before adopting any part of the report the government wishes to give it the most careful consideration and also wishes to consider its impact on Canada as a whole and on the taxpayers as a whole. We wish to do something which will not be just a stopgap, which will not be just a palliative, but something which will help railway transportation in Canada in the years ahead, and I do not think there is any government so well qualified to do it as the present one.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with interest to the minister during the last hour, and all that he has said does not make sense, and especially is that true of what he said in the last five minutes. Here is the situation. For 14 months the "non-ops" had been in negotiation with the C.N.R. and the C.P.R. and they could get no agreement whatsoever. They were prepared to settle for 14

cents but asked for 25, but they could get no satisfaction whatsoever from the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific. They could get no satisfaction from the railways, so right in the last hours the government brought in legislation not to give the "non-ops" any increase but to prevent a strike. The men carried on for a period of six months during which they could not strike. We read reports in the newspapers about what was supposed to be going on but we could get no answer from the Prime Minister or the government side as to what was taking place.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING NUMBER OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
The resolution before the committee is to approve the introduction of a bill to amend the Canadian National Railways Act which would increase the number of directors of the company from seven to 12.
The committee will recall that the third and final report of last year's sessional committee on railways, air lines and shipping recommended that the government might consider the advisability of strengthening the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways by adding to its present number. In the light of this unanimous recommendation, the government reached the conclusion that parliament should be asked to pass the appropriate legislation. The increase to 12 will
Canadian National Railways Act provide for broader representation on the board, and I feel sure the resolution will commend itself to the committee.
With the permission of the committee, I should like to make a short review of the history of the board of directors of the Canadian National Railway Company. Chapter 13, statutes of Canada, 1919, authorized the organization of the Canadian National Railway Company to operate the Canadian Northern Railway lines, the Canadian Government Railway lines and any other railway lines as should be entrusted to it from time to time by order in council.
The statute provided that the directors be appointed by the governor in council and their number was to be not less than five and not more than 15. Chapter 6, statutes of Canada, 1931, provided for the possible appointment of 17 directors instead of 15 as originally limited by chapter 13 of the statutes of 1919.
Order in council P.C. 2094 of October 4, 1922 appointed nine directors of the Canadian National Railway Company to fulfil the intentions of the above-mentioned legislation. The railway was operated with nine directors in 1923, and in 1924, the directors were increased to 13 and remained at 13 until December 24, 1930, at which time two additional directors were appointed making a total of 15. In 1931 two additional directors were appointed bringing the total to 17. From 1932 to December 30, 1933, the board consisted of 16 directors.
Chapter 33 of the statutes of Canada, 1933, being the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act, authorized the governor in council to vacate the existing board of directors of the Canadian National Railway Company and to appoint in their place three trustees. A board of trustees were appointed effective from December 30, 1933, consisting of three trustees under the chairmanship of the Hon. Charles Fullerton to replace the board of directors. This board functioned until October 1, 1936.
Under chapter 25, statutes of Canada, 1936, the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act was amended which authorized the governor in council to replace the board of trustees of the Canadian National Railway Company by seven directors.
The seven directors were appointed October 1, 1936, and the number of directors has remained at seven up to the present date. Since the amendment of the Canadian National Railways Act in 1955, the authority for appointment of the board of directors of the railway has been included therein, being section 6 of chapter 29, statutes of 1955.
Under the present legislation the directors are appointed by the governor in council for a term not exceeding three years but a director at any time may be removed for cause.

Canadian National Railways Act The salaries of the directors are paid by Canadian National Railways and the amount is fixed by the governor in council.
Mr. Chairman, as I said earlier in my statement, the increase in the number of directors to 12 will provide for broader representation on the board. If we look at the boards of directors of major railways in North America and the mileage operated by these railways, we find that the Canadian National Railways is certainly in an anomalous position in that it has a very small number of directors for the mileage it operates.
As hon. members know, there are seven directors on the board of directors of Canadian National Railways. This railway operates 26,329 miles. If we compare this with Canadian Pacific Railway, they have a board of 24 directors and operate 17,000 miles.
If we look at the short list I have here, the Baltimore & Ohio Railroad Company has 12 directors and operates only 7,000 miles. The New York Central Railroad Company has 15 directors and operates 14,000 miles. The Pennsylvania Railroad Company has 18 directors and operates 16,000 miles. The Southern Pacific Company has 16 directors and operates 13,000 miles. The Union Pacific Railroad Company has 17 directors and operates 11,000 miles.
This shows that of the six railways I have listed, the one with the smallest board of directors is the Baltimore & Ohio Railroad Company, with 12 directors, and it operates only about one quarter of the mileage operated by Canadian National Railways.
Therefore I think this proposal of the government will certainly help the Canadian National Railways' management in that it will give broader geographic representation and also a broader representation as far as the average Canadian activity is concerned.

Canadian National Railways Act are correct or not, I do not know, but let us assume that there has been at least-

I was going on to say that from the figures I have been able to obtain it appears that there has been a diminution or attrition in the number of employees of Canadian National Railways of at least 5,000 per year in the last four years. Yet while this is going on the government is increasing the number of directors. While men are being laid off directors are being added to the board. While men are without work directors are being increased on the board. While men are without employment on Canadian National Railways, it takes more men to administer the railway.
There has also been a fairly substantial reorganization of the various districts of Canadian National Railways recently. I am told this is in an effort to curtail expenditure, a move, incidentally, which is extremely unpopular with the men and with the public. On one occasion the hon. member for Levis gave some indication of what the railway reorganization has meant in his area and how this move has upset the workers in that region and changed the pattern which had existed for many, many years. Notwithstanding that reorganization, it is still found necessary by the government to increase the board of directors.
The deficit of Canadian National Railways this year is probably one of the highest in its history. The estimate given for 1961 is not too encouraging. What it will be I am unable to say but it will certainly be substantial, and if the recommendations of the royal commission on transportation or part thereof are not implemented then, of course, the deficit will reach astronomical figures. While that position exists in the Canadian National Railways the government thinks it is necessary to have more directors look after the business of the company.


If you have a small board such as exists now it seems to me that each director will take a greater responsibility than if there are more directors. It seems to me that each director will feel that he has a greater share of the responsibility if there are seven such directors than if there are 12. There is, of course, another very serious matter to which consideration must be given and that is territorial representation. That question is inevitably going to arise if the directorship is increased. This question is going to arise if the number of directors is such that there is likely to be more than one representative for each province, and that is, of course, what is going to happen here. Twelve directors will mean that there will be more than one director for each province. When there is one director from each province it seems to me that unquestionably there is a solemn duty to represent the interests of that province without, of course, neglecting the national interest. If there are two from a province you may well find that sectional divisions will arise.
Then there is the question of the representation of the province of Quebec if there are 12 directors. With 12 directors it will be expected that the province of Quebec will be accorded equitable representation having regard to its population. If it does not get such representation I need hardly tell the minister that he will hear about it in due course because he has repeatedly stated that the C.N.R. was not fair and just to his province. I am not going to put on the record the statement he has made. I have used it before and I do not think this is the opportune time to repeat it. But I do tell him that with these additional five directors he will be face to face with the problem of additional representation in his own province, whether there will be three directors or whether there will be less, and he will have to meet that problem.
It seems to me that the directors ought to be appointed from the point of view of their competence rather than from the point of view of geographical and political interests. There is no doubt that with 12 directors there will have to be geographical representation, and, so far as political interest is concerned, if the same pattern is followed here as is followed elsewhere I suppose that consideration will be given to that as well.

There are some who say that the Canadian Pacific Railway has a large board of directors and why should not Canadian National Railways likewise have a large board? I think there is a very important distinction to be drawn here between a crown corporation such as Canadian National Railways and national corporations. I believe they think it is necessary to have larger boards but in my opinion that is not so in the case of Canadian National Railways. Directors are appointed to the board of the Canadian Pacific Railway for various and obvious reasons. I can think of one such directors, whose name I shall not mention, who has been appointed to the Canadian Pacific board because of the tremendous business that will ensue to that railway, and I presume that applies to others too. From all this it seems to me that a great distinction exists between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways.
The question of regional representation, which I mentioned in passing a moment ago, is also of considerable importance. If you have two or more directors from a region or two directors from a province there is likely to be a clash of interests which would not exist if there were but one from the province or one from a region. For these and other reasons which will be submitted to the committee on behalf of the opposition we will oppose this measure.

Canadian National Railways Act

It would be a free enterprise company which would operate outside of the control of the department. The minister would report to parliament on behalf of the company but would have nothing to say about its operations. This provision was made in order to give the company all the advantages of a free enterprise operation and to keep it free of restrictions. But they did come up with this operation which has all the advantages of free enterprise and has none of the disadvantages, not one. In a free enterprise system, if your management is not competent or if your management does not produce the results you wish you change them, because they report to the shareholders and the shareholders are interested in the efficient operation of the company.
In this case, the management reports to the executive committee and if the executive committee is not in agreement with the management, management can change that executive committee. The executive committee of the Canadian National Railways are three, and they need not be the same three except for the president. The executive committee of the Canadian Pacific are seven out of a total board of directors of 24. We have on the C.N.R. three out of a total board of seven. If you wish to talk about the officers you find that in the C.N.R. we have 43 officers and in the C.P.R. we have 19 officers. If you want to talk about railway operations only, leaving out ancillary operations of the C.P.R., and if you wish to compare the railway operations, what do you find? This is what you find, and I will give the round figures. In the C.N.R. in 1960 there was total operating revenue of $963 million; operating expenses, $955 million; net revenue, $7.5 million. The C.P.R. in the same period, 1960, there were revenues of $457 million; expenses of $423 million and net earnings of close to $34 million. If you want to go back to 1959, you find on the C.N.R. $740 million on the revenue side, $720 million on the expenses side and $19 million on the revenue side. Mr. Chairman, I think the ground has been pretty fully covered and there is very little left for me to say. I wish to say at the outset that I am in favour of increasing the number of directors. Indeed, as another hon. member has already said, I would be very glad if the number of directors were raised above the present proposed number.
There are two reasons, I think, for having directors. One is that if the Almighty is

kind you may get directors who are helpful in the management of the railway. The other more obvious and more certain reason is that if you are wise in your appointments you will get people who, by their prestige, and so on, will raise the reputation of the railway in the eyes of the business community and who through their business connections will bring business to the railway.
The hon. member for Port Arthur has pointed this out. He has said that perhaps it is not a situation that we think is ideal, but at any rate it is practical and inevitable and there is nothing improper about it. Incidentally, I can see no reason whatsoever why a crown corporation should not make full use of directors just as well as a private corporation.
In the authority we have set up for a national productivity council we have tried to get the best businessmen we can and the best labour men we can. They have been glad to come and serve.
I am not going to go through the objections which the hon. member for Laurier raised, except for one or two. I did find it difficult to follow him when he said that because this is a time of unemployment we should not be increasing the expenses of the railway.
No one wants to increase them by a dollar, of course. However, what we are talking about would at the most mean a few tens of thousands of dollars; perhaps less than that. If we were wise and got people who were worth their salt, they might very well make suggestions and bring business which would result in hundreds of thousands, and perhaps millions of dollars of business being brought to the railway. If I may say so with deference to the hon. member for Laurier, his point in this respect seemed to me to be quite unreal.
One thing he did not say, which I was glad he did not say and I was afraid he might say, was that these appointments will be political, and will not be good appointments.
In my opinion the appointments that have been made are excellent. Mr. E. W. Bickle died regretted by everybody. I think he was a great asset to the railway. We have no reason to think that we will not get other men of the same calibre. If we can get such people, we should do so, and I do not see any reason why we should not. People like this would play a real part in building up the railway.
One point has been made which is real and which should not be ignored. I know nothing about this, but I think this statement was made by the hon. member for Laurier. The hon. member said that the full-time officials of the railway would not be so keen to get additions to the board.

Mr. Chairman, we have heard an interesting political speech by the hon. member for Laurier. I must say that the Liberal party must be getting right down to the bottom of the barrel to try and make political advantage of a simple measure like this. But everybody certainly on this side of the house, and I am sure this applies to the hon. member for Port Arthur, is trying to do something about the C.N.R. to make it a more efficient operation.
I, too, have sat on the sessional committee. It was my understanding that this was a unanimous recommendation of the committee. Certainly we are very sorry that the hon. member for Laurier could not be there for all the committee meetings. However, at the same time we have to spend some time in these committees, we bring in recommendations and we are very pleased to see the government accepting this one.
I do not accept his premise that the management of the C.N.R. should be asked whether or not they would like an addition to the board of directors. It is my contention that perhaps we need a stronger, more efficient board of directors. I like the suggestion put forward by the hon. member for Vancouver South, of an effective and perhaps little larger executive committee to scrutinize the decisions made by the officers of the C.N.R.
I think enough has been said about the foolishness of the argument of the hon. member for Laurier with regard to unemployment. I have one other remark I should like to interject here, that they have enough vice presidents now in the C.N.R. that they could lay off half a dozen without missing them very much. If they added some competent men from various parts of the country this might very well have the effect of providing management the stimulus that is required to make this railway run more efficiently, and to improve public relations, both with employees and members of the public, assisting the taxpayers in their problem of running this state owned railway.
I thought it rather amazing that the hon. member for Port Arthur, being the good socialist that he is, was apparently having a few agonizing pains because the free enterprise operation of the Canadian Pacific

Canadian National Railways Act Railway was better. I think one of the reasons why that fact exists is because the management of the Canadian National Railways has, like some senior civil servants, been burdened by red tape. They might be able to do a more efficient job if they were aware of the fact that there was to be a searching inquiry made by a sessional committee of the House of Commons. In this regard, I am sure it will come to pass that we will acquire greater detailed information in respect of the operations of the railway, because this is the only overriding scrutiny to which management is subject. Apparently another reason why the hon. member for Laurier spoke today against an increase in the directorship of the Canadian National Railways was because there had been reorganization of the railroads in respect of several districts, and for some reason or other it would be detrimental to this organization to have an increase in the directorship.
I am unable to follow his thinking in that regard, because it seems to me that with this reorganization, it is vitally important that we have an increase in the board of directors. I am thinking particularly in regard to railway companies operating in northern Alberta. The Northern Alberta Railways is 50 per cent owned by the Canadian National Railways and very seldom has any representation on the Canadian National Railways' board of directors, yet the N.A.R. management makes decisions, or does not make them, as the case may be, and there is no check in this regard.
It seems to me, as I said at the outset, that the Liberal party, particularly the hon. member for Laurier, has been more effective at other times when there was something to take issue with, but the hon. members of that party tonight have been on very flimsy ground when they suggest they are opposed to this proposed legislation because the representation would not be proper geographically. The hon. member for Laurier has tried the old dodge of divide and conquer-if things are not right in Quebec, or western Canada, or other places, it will be bad politically. This was the impression he left with me. I am very sorry he has created that impression because I think it is an extremely weak position on the part of the official opposition. I suggest that this government be commended for accepting the recommendations of the committee, and I personally hope it will continue to do so in future.

On the other hand, I think we both feel, as do most hon. members on this side of the house, that at a time when the president of the United States is visiting this country; at a time when we have the kind of economic crisis with which we are faced today in this country, we should be concerned with problems of more gravity. What have we been doing in this house today? In other words, we are being asked to sit these long hours, not to consider the grave situation which faces this country today, but to deal with trivial things like this.

I have explained to hon. gentlemen that I was speaking solely because of the speeches of the hon. gentleman for Vancouver South and the hon. gentleman for Jasper-Edson which really had nothing to do with whether there should be 12 directors or seven, but fundamentally were attacks on the management of the Canadian National Railways. What those hon. members have said is that the government is not doing its duty in supervising the Canadian National Railways properly; that the government was allowing the Canadian National Railways to get away with murder, and that is why they are supporting this bill. This is the inference I drew from the remarks made by those two hon. gentlemen. I do not want to be unfair to anyone, and if those hon. gentleman feel that is an unfair inference to draw they may say so. The hon. member for Vancouver South referred to the deficits of the Canadian National Railways which were getting higher and higher. I suggest there is nothing new about that situation because since there has been a Canadian National Railways, whenever there has been a Tory government, the deficits of that railway went higher and higher. Whether that is coincidence or cause and effect, I do not know, but it is the fact. I suggest the reason for that situation is that we have a Tory government rather than because we have seven instead of 12 directors.

If the management of the Canadian National Railways is as bad as the hon. member for Vancouver South and Jasper-Edson say it is, the government ought to have guts enough to change it. I do not think it is as bad as that, but if it is, the government should have the guts to change it, and I suggest they will not be changing it very much by appointing 12 directors rather than seven. Probably all that will result from this change will be that five Tory heelers will now have something to do with their spare time.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I hate to follow speakers on the government side and to pour salt on the wounds which they have exposed under the intellectual armour of the hon. member for Laurier, but shall have to do so later. First, however, having listened to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate, I am amazed that-if he is really sincere in the position he takes, that this is a small trivial matter-he felt it was necessary to make any intervention at all in this debate.

speechtext:
The hon. member may have explained to the satisfaction of some members, but I doubt if the majority of hon. members of this committee have been satisfied.
Having heard the hon. member for Laurier earlier today, and again recently, in connection with the very grave problems which he relates to the railways of this country, I thought that any measure at all by which this government could attempt to remedy the situation would be acceptable. I suggest one way of doing that is to attack this problem by organizing some change in the administration of the C.N.R.
I was disappointed, as was the hon. member for Vancouver South, in the attitude taken by the hon. member for Laurier on two instances. I was disappointed first in the stand he took when he opened the discussion on behalf of the opposition and, second, having listened to the very logical and devastating argument made by the hon. member for Vancouver South, I was satisfied that the hon. member for Laurier, in his second statement tonight, was going to tell us he had changed his mind, and that he was now convinced that this was a good and logical bill which the opposition was now going to accept. I was very much surprised that he did not do this.
Mr. Chairman, I will deal first with two of the points which were raised by the hon. member for Laurier. He suggested, as a possible reason why this bill should not be introduced, the fact that the previous minister of transport was not convinced, at the
Canadian National Railways Act time it was discussed by the sessional committee last year, that this was an essential move. I do not know what took place in that committee, as I was not there, but will accept the statement read into the record by the hon. member. However, surely that is one of the trade-marks of this government and of this party'-it is prepared at any time to accept recommendations of a committee when it can be shown that changes in policy, in legislation, and in programs are necessary and desirable. That is the trade-mark of the progressive thinking of the Progressive Conservative party. When changes are required we are prepared to advocate them, to put them in the form of legislation and to place them in the statute books of the country.
Second, the hon. member for Laurier was somewhat critical of what he thought might be the calibre of any new appointments which might be made provided this resolution and the legislation which will be based on it are passed. I think this is a place where the hon. member and members of his party should be very sensitive. After all, when a party has held office for 22 years it becomes tottering, sluggish, lazy and complacent. I always think of that analogy of the line .of extinct volcanoes, which may well reflect the position of the previous government. That type of government is reflected in the appointments which they make. At this time I am certainly not going to specifically criticize the management of the Canadian National or any of the crown corporations, but in the dying days of a government which has held power for many years there is a tendency to make appointments which I fear are not in the best interests of the country; and certainly the balance sheet of the Canadian National Railways, as it has been presented to this House of Commons from year to year, is the best indication of this fact.
I think of a crown corporation where you have an executive who is a permanent member of the directorate and where you have other directors who meet from time to time. There is a strong tendency-the likelihood is most extreme-that as this board meets, the policies advocated by the executive will be passed down to the directors without too much consideration. There should a continual change of directors. There should be a board of directors whose attitude is, "I am from Missouri; I must be shown that this is right and proper". I am satisfied that there has been too little of that in the past. This is one of the reasons why the position of this crown corporation has come to where it is today. I think we need fresh blood, new thinking and a new approach.
I certainly would go along with those hon. members who have suggested that we might

Canadian National Railways Act seriously think of increasing the membership of the board of directors not to 12, but to a larger number. For example, I heard the hon. member for Jasper-Edson speak of the situation of the Northern Alberta Railway. That railway consists of approximately 1,400 miles, and for many years it has had no representation at all on the board of directors. This is an isolated but self-sufficient railway, and it should have some measure of representation on the board. I am not suggesting, for example, that 1,400 miles of railway, in relation to the total mileage of the C.N.R., would justify the Northern Alberta Railway having a separate director, or that the area which the Northern Alberta Railway serves ought to have a separate director, but this sort of reasoning seems to me sound and reasonable. We have not had enough of it in the past.
There is another reason I want to touch on as to the necessity for this change. Anyone who has examined the recommendations contained in the first report of the royal commission on transportation must be struck by their approach to this matter on a regional basis. For example, two of the recommendations which they make deal with the elimination in course of time of passenger traffic in certain areas and on certain lines where it has proven to be uneconomic. The same situation prevails also with regard to freight traffic in what they call low density traffic areas. The suggestion there is that an annual subsidy of $13 million should be payable over a period of 15 years. There has been a recommendation, also, that subsidies totalling some $62 million, subsequently scaled down in five years to 20 per cent of that amount, should be payable in respect of the elimination of the passenger traffic. Now surely, Mr. Chairman, that requires representation on the board of directors on a more varied, more regional basis so that those directors when they come to the board meetings should be able to reflect the thinking and the situation in their particular areas.
When it is necessary for the management of the Canadian National-and I assume the management of the Canadian Pacific-to make various applications to the board of transport commissioners with regard to the gradual elimination of those services, they should be made after adequate knowledge is brought to the board by a director or directors who have some indication of the feelings of the people in that area, who have some knowledge of the economic conditions and are prepared to place this knowledge and information and make their position clear in the board meetings. For this reason, if for no other, it is my sincere opinion that this legislation, when brought before the House of Commons, will

be most timely and will be very effective in helping the Canadian National Railways to deal with the very vexatious problems which will confront them if and when they are required to implement these portions of the MacPherson royal commission report.

Mr. Chairman, the ground has been pretty well gone over as to the merits of appointing a greater number of directors to the board of the Canadian National Railways. There were, however, a few remarks made by the hon. member for Laurier that caused me some concern. As I recollect his remarks, he said to the minister he did not think the fact that a committee had recommended this was much of a reason for going ahead and doing it. It is a well-known fact that under the previous government committees did not play the part that they are playing at the present time. It has been the aim of the Prime Minister and the present government to build up the amount of work done and the contribution made to our proceedings by committees.
I feel the members of the Liberal party must have some great concern about this because, after all, their own work was put into that committee; they had some members on the committee and during the time that we discussed this matter I do not recall any objection being taken by any one of them. The hon. member for Laurier said he was not there or he certainly would have objected. But none of the other members objected to it and they were there.
Of course, the report was made to the house and there was another opportunity if the opposition wanted to object to it, at that time. I find it strange that we have not heard from any of the members of that party who were on the committee and endorsed the report. I would have thought there would have been a little more freedom within the Liberal party now that they are out of office. We know that that party had some rigidity while they were in office. I would have thought that certainly a party in opposition would have a backbencher who would be free to stand in his place and say something. I say it is very unusual that we have not seen any members of the committee from that party stand up and either agree or disagree with the hon. member for Laurier. I think that a further contribution would be made to this debate if we heard from some of those members who sat with us on the committee. Are they now going to get up and tell us we wasted our time sitting there; that they do not really think committees are much use after all. I do hope the government is not going to be in any way influenced by them.

I am sure the members of the Conservative party commend the government for the action it took to strengthen our committees and to enable backbenchers of the house to make some contribution to the proceedings of the house.

I pointed out this afternoon that for ten years he has been coming before committees and in the past the best M.P.s in the house have taken him on and he has always been able to confound them. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM AMOUNT OF BANK LOANS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the purpose of this resolution is to permit the introduction of a bill to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act. The bill is very brief. In a word the amendment provides for an increase of $100 million in the aggregate principal amount of guaranteed loans which may be made by all of the chartered banks during the existing lending period, April 1, 1959, to June 30, 1962.

The limit on guaranteed loans under the act now established in the legislation for this period is $300 million, and it is proposed to increase that amount to $400 million. From April 1, 1959, which is the commencement date of the current lending period, until February 28 last a total of 134,200 loans had been made amounting in round figures to $194 million. Lending has exceeded earlier expectations and there remains just over $100 million in this authorized lending pool for the remaining 16 months of this present term. If present lending trends continue, this amount will be insufficient to cover the total of loans which may be made between now and the end of the lending period.
The amendment is designed to ensure that an adequate supply of credit will be available to Canadian farmers for farm improvement purposes under the legislation. Hon. members will, I am sure, be gratified to know that the credit facilities provided by the act have proved so valuable and have been so widely used by Canadian farmers. I might refer hon. members to the annual report under the act for the year 1960, which has been tabled. The report indicates that there has been a substantial increase in lending during recent years and that the total of loans for 1960 of approximately $102 million represents an all-time annual record.
The bill to be founded upon the resolution, Mr. Chairman, is very brief. It will change one word in the act. This is the word "three" in section 5(d) of the act as amended in 1959 by chapter 25 of the statutes of that year. The bill will change the word "three" to "four".

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM AMOUNT OF BANK LOANS
speechtext: The Minister of Finance, I am sure, will be gratified to learn that for once I quite agree wholeheartedly with something he is doing in this house. We on this side of the house are exceedingly proud of this piece of legislation which was part of the reconstruction program introduced by the Mackenzie King government and by that great finance minister, Hon. J. L. Ilsley, at the end of the war. The fact that this legislation is continuing to serve the Canadian people well, particularly that community to which it was directed, and has served as a model for another bill the minister introduced earlier this session that we also had pleasure in supporting, is I think a matter of gratification to a party which, according to the Globe and Mail, provides the ideas in this house.

speechtext:
I rise to express our support for this resolution. I might say that we are rather pleased to notice that the minister comes before the committee, according to the act, to get authority to guarantee this 10 per cent of the additional funds that are required.

We are very glad that they are required. We support this measure wholeheartedly because it has played a very important part in the years since it was first made effective in assisting and developing the economic family farm. I think the experience of the administration since the act was given effect proves this piece of legislation has been very valuable to the farmers in this country who needed short term or intermediate credit.
I know quite a number of farmers in my own constituency who have utilized this act. I see that, according to the report, the purposes of the loans are, the purchase of implements-there is a considerable increase in that

the improvement and renovation of farm buildings; the purchase of livestock; the clearing and breaking of land-this is a section in which I am particularly interested and I will come back to it in a few minutes -and miscellaneous developments. According to the report, a remarkably low loss ratio is shown, about one tenth of 1 per cent. I think that is a remarkably low loss ratio. When the minister replies, I should like him to inform the committee what the loss ratio is on commercial loans from the banks under ordinary circumstances. The comparison would be very interesting. I think the loss ratio demonstrates the stability of the investments and the fact that the money is being loaned wisely.
First of all, I want to make a suggestion that I have made previously in connection with the clearing and breaking of land. I believe that farmers who borrow money to clear and break land should receive the same exemptions for the money expended in that direction as the gas and pipe line companies or oil companies receive under the Income Tax Act on the basis that they are bringing natural resources into production. I do urge the minister to give some consideration to this suggestion. I think the farmer who increases our agricultural production by breaking or clearing land, draining land or in some cases diking land, should receive the same consideration as these other companies under the Income Tax Act. I feel there are valid reasons for the consideration of these representations.
I should like to ask the minister if he has received any representations or suggestions from farm organizations in the last year in respect of the improvement of the administration of this act.

speechtext:
The hon. member has asked about several points. As hon. members are aware, this legislation has been in existence now for some 17 years. It has been amended from time to time. It was originally introduced with a limit on the term of years for which it was in effect and with, of course, a ceiling on the extent of crown liability. This period has been moved forward. As the hon. member will recall, in 1959 we brought amendments before the house and those amendments enlarged the scope of the act. They moved forward the lending period. They fixed the total of permissible loans at $300 million and enlarged the maximum individual loan from the figure of $5,000, as it had been previously, to $7,500. These amendments have been very well received and have undoubtedly proved their usefulness to the Canadian people.
As to making the available facilities of the act known, I think it may be said that the facilities of this legislation are well known to the Canadian farmer today. It is a well established credit facility available to him. Pamphlets have been available through the rural branches of the chartered banks for a long time explaining the features of the act and the facilities that are available under its terms to the farmer.
The hon. member asks about the way in which the guarantee is administered. The act, of course, stipulates the total of loans that may be made in pursuance of its provisions. This total is not a revolving fund. It is a total of loans permitted in the particular lending period. In the earlier years of the act these were three-year periods. In 1959 we made the present period of three years and three months in order to bring it to June 30, 1962, which was thought to be a more convenient date for the house in the course of its sittings. The legislation fixes the extent of the crown's liability as guarantor in the 10 per cent provision which is to be found in section 4, subsection 1 of the act.
As to the guarantee itself, these loans, of course, are made by the banks and the individual branch bank is responsible for reviewing the suitability of the applicant and his eligibility for a loan. The ordinary tests as to credit worthiness of the applicant are in the hands of the local branch managers to enforce. Then the loans made under the act by the bank are reported to the department. Regular reports are submitted to the department and a record is kept there of the loans. There must be a record, of course, in order
[Mr. Herridge.l

to be sure that the operations are carried on within the limits of and according to the terms established by the legislation.
When a default occurs it is, of course, the responsibility of the lending bank concerned to endeavour to enforce the terms of the loan. It is only when the bank has failed in its efforts to remedy the default that the claim would be made in pursuance of the guarantee. When the claim is made on the guarantee it is only after the bank has exhausted its normal remedies in its endeavours to collect, that the loan liability would be discharged by the guarantor, namely the crown. In that event the crown is subrogated to the rights of the lending bank so that if there were opportunity for recovery against the borrower, in that case the crown would be in a position to exercise the rights that had previously accrued to the bank under the terms of the loan. That is the procedure.
The hon. member for Kootenay West has pointed out the loss record under this legislation as being quite a remarkable one. The 1960 annual report at page 4 contains this instructive paragraph:
Losses under this legislation continue to be low. During the year-
That is the year 1960.
-209 claims for a total of $167,406 were paid. Since the inception of the legislation 1,752 claims have been paid for a total of $1,192,594. On the basis of a total of $1,013,782,362 lent, the loss ratio is approximately one tenth of 1 per cent.
Recoveries of claims paid to date amount to $100,605.
To paraphrase what has been there stated in the report, the aggregate of loans made under this legislation since 1944 exceeds $1 billion. Yet in the 16 years of operation the number of claims on which default has been made with a resulting claim under the guarantee is just 1,752. The crown has paid in pursuance of its guarantees a total of $1,192,594; and the crown having paid out under its guarantees sums totalling that figure has made recoveries of $100,605.
