Recently, in other places connected with this house we have been told that this is a most wonderful piece of legislation, although possibly a little bit less than what it could be. I may say frankly that I refer to certain machine companies in certain discussions with regard to farm machinery prices. Time and time again it was stated by those particular companies that this very act itself had contributed much to the welfare of Canadian agriculture in particular. Their only comment was that it did not go quite far enough. I repeat what I said previously. I am very happly to bring this matter to the attention of the committee. The final over-all figure is increased.
There again I would call this statement to the attention of the very quiet group in the corner. They have so often talked about interest rates. On several occasions in the committee it was pointed out to us, and very reluctantly as a matter of fact, that the equipment companies do make arrangements to finance farm machinery purchases, and of course the rates of interest are from 10 to 11 per cent.
Mr. Chairman, in rising tonight in committee to support this measure we all realize that the rate of interest is 5 per cent. Most certainly we must all commend the government for increasing the total amount available under this measure to Canadian agriculture for the purchase of farm machinery, livestock and all the way down the line.
This means more aid and more support to Canadian agriculture, which particularly relates-and I again endorse some of the things said by hon. members who have spoken before me in this committee-to the small family farm. This question has come up so many times previously that I am not going to go into it and take the time of the committee tonight. However, by way of emphasis I should again like to say that this increase in the total amount most certainly enlarges the aid to and contributes to the betterment of the family farmer in Canada.

I am speaking about western Canada, yes. The figure I referred to was given to the committee. I do not know that it applied particularly to western Canada.
However, there has been growing up in recent years a practice by farm implement companies themselves to finance a very substantial proportion of their own farm implement sales.
This is of course important to them and it is important to the dealers, because it makes it possible for them to make sales that perhaps otherwise would not be made. But it is very expensive for the farmer; it means a higher cost for the financing of farm implements. We were told the rates were in the neighbourhood of 12 per cent, and certainly to finance farm implements through the farm implement companies themselves would cost twice as much-perhaps more than twice as much-as the cost under this legislation.
I think it is very much in order that we should increase the total amount of money that may be loaned under this act in the hope that the banks will be lenient, that they will promote this kind of loan, and that the implement companies and the farmers will make use of these facilities. I think there is probably a tendency on the part of banks to make loans with guaranteed higher interest rates, although I understand they have changed this policy. I certainly think it is correct to say, with the existence of policy generally restricting bank credit, banks will put the squeeze or lid on this kind of loan, and enforce the same kind of control as is enforced in respect of other types of loans.
This is good legislation and should be continued. I feel there will be ample money available under the act to cover loan needs of agricultural producers. I repeat again now, something which I have stated in discussions of this type of measure in the past, that I feel very strongly that guarantees which are given to banks, under this and other legislation, should be given to credit unions.
The minister may say that credit unions have not asked for this type of legislation. He may also say, as he has said before, that credit unions are not under the jurisdiction of the federal government. He may be able to give many reasons why he disagrees with the suggestion I have made. I made this

proposal when another bill was before the house guaranteeing bank loans to small businesses, and the minister of finance, of that day, said that credit union spokesmen and representatives had not asked for this type of guarantee. I feel those representatives were a little slow and not perhaps completely up to date regarding the matter, because after that legislation had gone through the House of Commons and was before the banking committee of the other place, representatives of a co-operative union said that under certain circumstances they would like these guarantees to apply to them. While the minister was absolutely right when he said that credit unions had not asked for this guarantee, they did ask for-not full guarantees across the board-guarantees under certain circumstances. I am sure the day will arrive when guarantees under this kind of legislation will be given to credit unions. I think the fact of the matter is that not only has the government itself been reluctant to provide this type of guarantee, the credit unions themselves have been slow in asking for it and in coming to the conclusion that it should apply to them.

Some
Farm Improvement Loans Act charge about 7 per cent interest, but they pay patronage dividends. They pay dividends to the individuals who borrow the money. However, I do feel that credit unions, at least under certain circumstances, would be able to lend money at this rate of interest, but they should be allowed to speak for themselves. I look forward to the day when credit unions in this country are given the same kind of guarantees as are given to banks. I look forward to the day when credit unions occupy an even larger portion of the lending field and, in fact, become the people's bank, owned and operated by membership, and feel that when that day arrives they will carry out a very useful service providing money at rates of interest certainly lower than the rates of interest now being charged by small loans companies after having paid dividends. I refer to interest rates much lower than those charged now by implement companies.
I suggest also that banks should be more lenient in the provision of loans under this act. I feel it is a disgrace to the banking system, to the government and to parliament, that institutions, charging interest rates of 10 or 12 per cent, should be occupying, to a larger and larger degree, that area of farm implement lending.
The interest rate provided by this legislation is very reasonable. The resolution which was introduced when the last amendments to this act were made did not initially contain a limit on interest of 5 per cent. Some hon. members worked very hard to have the 5 per cent limit placed in that legislation, and we are very glad that this has been done, and feel this is the kind of interest rate that should be provided.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words about this resolution. I believe this is wonderful legislation. Increasing money for loans from $300 million to $400 million will be of great assistance to the young farmers in the Peace river district of my constituency. In that area we have 1 million fertile acres, the finest land in the world. Wheat grown in that area has five times won the championship of the world at the Chicago exhibition, which finally barred one Herman Trellee from entering a sample from the Peace river country.
Not long ago we had people from the United States coming into the area buying up the ranch land. Young farmers want to

Farm Improvement Loans Act buy their fathers out because they have cultivated the land, worked it and know exactly how to farm it. They wish to stay in the farming business and, to do so, like to buy out the old man, and the old man wants to go into town to retire. These old gentlemen are in the age group that I am in, around 70, and are getting too old to do the hard work, and the young fellows want to take over. Naturally they want to take over those farms on which they have been raised and have made a living and the farming methods for which they understand. I suggest that no one is a better farmer than the boy who has been raised on the farm.
The Peace river country, as I have said, is wonderful country consisting of a million acres. When I look out over the Ottawa countryside and see this stony land it makes my heart bleed. These are good hard working people, and that country would be an asset to Canada. Land is a thing that is needed. We need more money. The sum of $400 million is fine, but let us get it up to $500 million.
Like the last speaker, I think the co-operatives should come under this legislation. We have one of the largest co-operatives in Canada at Dawson Creek. Hon. members can check and see whether I am right. Some hon. members laugh, but we have the largest cooperative store in Canada. We are not out in the bush, you know; we are located in the finest farming country you ever saw. Those people came in just the other day with 2,600 ewes. They lost 14 bringing them in. If we can kill off New Zealand in so far as their lambs are concerned, why we can raise all of the lambs necessary for all of western and eastern Canada.
I just wish to compliment the minister on this fine resolution and I hope we get more money still. Thank you.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM AMOUNT OF BANK LOANS
speechtext:
I should like to say a few words on this particular resolution. I realize that it may well be a necessity because of the amount of loans made in the past two years. The sum of $98 million was borrowed in 1959 and $101 million in 1960. If another $100 million, or a little more, is loaned in the coming year we shall well exceed the limit which, as I understand it, is now $300 million. Therefore this legislation is certainly a necessity. The maximum amount must be increased to $400 million.
In looking over the report of the farm improvement loans board tabled in the house by the minister I find that on page 7 it suggests that the banks have given the fullest co-operation toward meeting the credit requirements of agriculture generally. Before the committee on agriculture the farm implement dealers suggested that as early as

May 1959 they sought other ways to provide credit for farmers to purchase agricultural machinery. This is interesting because in 1958 this government increased the amount of the loans, as has been mentioned already, from $5,000 to $7,500. It is interesting to note on page 10 of the 1960 annual report that the loans jumped from $69 million in 1957 to $90 million in 1958, to $98 million in 1959 and to $101 million in 1960.
Five years before the maximum was increased the maximum amount loaned out in any one year never exceeded $70 million. Certainly, the extension of the amount loanable from $5,000 to $7,500 did give quite an advantage to a large number of farmers with respect to the amount of the loan for the purchase of agricultural machinery. It certainly was welcomed by the machine companies themselves.
I had grave doubts, Mr. Chairman, and wondered whether perhaps this would not simply allow the well established farmer to borrow more money. I am pleased to see that, according to the annual report of 1960, at page 4, there were 28,774 borrowers who had not previously obtained farm improvement loans. I think this is a welcome figure and it accounts for 42 per cent of the number of loans made. Therefore, I might suggest that perhaps new farmers are coming into the borrowing field at all times, and perhaps more farmers are taking advantage of the Farm Improvement Loans Act.
I might say that at times I have been a bit disturbed about how this legislation is administered and how the operations of some banks have limited the amount of the loan under the act. I notice in the 1959 report that the Bank of Commerce loaned less money in 1959 than in 1958. It was one of those banks that was perhaps lending money, or lending a greater share of its money, to more lucrative business. I think that to a greater extent the banks could lend money to farmers who, through necessity or a desire to get ahead, have branched out and accepted part-time jobs besides their farm work. Some banks have a tendency to limit loans to this type of parttime farmer, and other tenant farmers have found it difficult to borrow money because they do not have a secure title to the land. They may have a long term lease of it, but the banks have been reluctant to lend to them because in the next year or two they may be somewhere else or in some other farming community or district.
I notice that on page 7 of the annual report it is suggested that the terms of the loans and the rate are 5 per cent per annum. The hon. member for Assiniboia suggested that when this measure was brought into the house in 1958 there was some suggestion of changing

the interest rate. Well, he was mixed up as usual. What he was referring to was the Farm Credit Corporation and not the Farm Improvement Loans Act. I am not really surprised because the hon. member for Assiniboia has been taken in this house to be an agricultural expert. But he is so far away from the farm that I do not think he could tell a tractor from a combine, let alone a kernel of wheat from a kernel of barley. Therefore, it is quite normal to expect him to get mixed up between a Farm Credit Corporation loan and a farm improvement loan, which are two different things entirely. The one is a loan from the government, the other is a loan through the bank for a smaller amount, mainly toward the purchase of machinery.
The hon. member went on to talk about credit unions and co-operatives taking advantage of this legislation. I do not think there would be any objection to that if they became a chartered bank and loaned at the same interest rate. I do know the farmers would welcome another lending institution from which to borrow. I know the credit unions are sometimes short of lending money but some of the large co-operatives have quite a bit and are able to back a lot of insurance companies and so on, particularly those in Saskatchewan. Therefore, they might well have the financial resources to enable them to become a chartered bank, or set up a chartered bank and get under this act. I do not know, but I would welcome it if they did.
One of the things that I should like to see taken into greater consideration under this act while they are expanding the amount to be loaned under it is a change in the attitude of banks toward lending money toward the purchase of machinery. Some of the banks have a tendency to lend money toward the purchase of new machinery or practically new machinery. I know it is difficult for a farmer. He might see a tractor that is five years old. A lot of five year old tractors are pretty good machines and they could be picked up at pretty reasonable prices; but it is sometimes difficult for a farmer to get a farm improvement loan on a five year old tractor. Banks are a little hesitant about putting out the money. They would like to see the farmer purchase a new tractor, and they would give a farm improvement loan on a new tractor. But oftentimes a farmer can borrow a lot cheaper on a five year old tractor and he can buy it a lot cheaper. I realize that you can pick up many lines of machinery that are one, two, three years old. But when you get in the five to ten year class, a lot of bankers are very reluctant to lend under this act on these particular types of machines.
I also notice in the annual report that a greater number of loans are being made for
Farm, Improvement Loans Act livestock. Actually, in the past three or four years, whether we like it or not, the cow has become a very stable sort of financial investment for farmers, particularly in western Canada and, I might say, in all of Canada. There is no safer place to invest a dollar bill than in a cow. I think the banks could make a substantially greater amount of loans toward livestock purchases. Recently a lot of feeder associations have been established which are making loans for the purchase of livestock by cattle feeders and other farmers who wish to purchase livestock but these farmers must pay 6J per cent on the borrowed money. If they could borrow the money under the Farm Improvement Loans Act they would only have to pay 5 per cent interest and the cattle would be theirs. If they decided to keep them for an extra year they would not run into any difficulty if they met their payments on their loans and they would have a greater length of time to pay the money.
I notice that farm improvement loans are repayable within four years but that the maximum period is ten years. I must say that in my experience of farm improvement loans the limit in most cases has been three years although with the extension in the amount that can be borrowed from $5,000 to $7,500 the banks have tried to extend the period to four years and possibly five years. I think it would be a very rare exception where they would extend the period to the maximum of ten years and I wonder how many times they have actually done so.
I was interested in learning that before the agricultural committee one of the farm machinery companies had suggested that 38 per cent of the machines purchased through their dealers in western Canada last year were financed by their own finance company. To me this was a surprising and shocking statement because these farmers were borrowing money at an interest rate of 11 per cent. I would think that if the banks were willing to co-operate and lend to the fullest extent on new and used machinery the great field of machinery financing into which the machinery companies are stepping would be absorbed under the Farm Improvement Loans Act.
Some members may wonder why I emphasize a greater amount of lending for secondhand farm machinery. Today in western Canada, and I think the same holds true for all of Canada, I know that there are two secondhand tractors sold for every new one or possibly three or four in the case of some dealers. Therefore when I look at the annual report and see that 26,000 tractors were purchased last year I wonder how many of those were used machines and how many were new. With respect to used machinery

Farm Improvement Loans Act particularly, the finance companies which are part and parcel of the machine companies are moving into this field at a rapid rate. In fact, some dealers have told me that the only way they can move stock is to find somebody whose credit rating at the bank is not good enough and who is willing to take secondhand machinery such as they have on their lots at the company's terms, which means an interest rate of 11 per cent. Therefore I think the greatest area for expansion under the Farm Improvement Loans Act is to give greater consideration in the case of secondhand machinery and also in the case of livestock loans and permitting farmers to purchase livestock on a three-year basis. To my way of thinking this would be very helpful to anybody wanting to purchase what might be termed a basic herd. Three years is a relatively short period to pay for a basic herd and this period could well be lengthened to the maximum of ten years if the farmer had that kind of credit rating.
A few years ago livestock prices were fluctuating a little more than is the case today. The farmers of western Canada all remember the foot and mouth disease outbreak and the drastic drop in cattle prices after that occurrence. Today, however, there is a floor price on cattle and the market will not depress completely. Therefore there is not nearly the risk in investing money in cattle that there was in 1952 when a great number of feeders in western Canada went completely bankrupt because there was no floor under cattle and prices dropped substantially.
I have very little more to say than that I hope the banks will make a real effort to extend credit in the areas I and other members have mentioned tonight. I hope that the farmers will take greater advantage of the 5 per cent interest rate rather than turning to the finance companies set up by the machinery companies. Last year and in years past the finance companies have been making substantial profits. It might be interesting to note that Traders Finance made as much money as the average chartered bank in Canada.

Farm Improvement Loans Act want to say that it is doing a grand job in the farming areas of western Canada.
I should like to add a word or two on the need for a greater amount of intermediate credit. The period of the loan should be extended perhaps by a year or two. In other words, the great need of the farm population is intermediate credit. On many occasions bank managers who make loans are inclined to squeeze down the period of repayment of the loan and to make it too short for the farmer to make a return on his operations and repay the loan. I would suggest that if there is one thing the Minister of Finance might take up with the banks, it would be the lengthening of the period of repayment of the loans in order to cope adequately with the need for intermediate credit.
There is one other point I should like to make. The regulations which are written by the farm improvement loan administration contain a provision permitting the bank manager to make loans for the purchase of new buildings. Further along in the same regulations there is a provision which permits bank managers to make loans for the purchase of secondhand buildings. These two provisions are set apart in the regulations. I found in one instance that a mistake had been made by one of the banks in that they turned down the request of a farmer for a loan to purchase a secondhand building. At Claresholm, Alberta, several buildings were offered for sale by the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation. The bank manager in one nearby town turned down a request for a loan simply because he did not read far enough in the regulations to ascertain that a loan could be made under a later section in the regulations.
My only purpose in mentioning this incident is to make a constructive suggestion to the Minister of Finance. When the regulations are rewritten, it would be helpful to have a cross reference on these two particular sections, the one dealing with authority to purchase new buildings and the other dealing with authority to purchase secondhand buildings. These two sections should be brought together by some kind of cross reference in order to avoid the possibility of bank managers making mistakes. I thought I should take up the matter with the Minister of Finance because this cross reference would make a very worth-while addition to any new regulations issued for the guidance of bank managers.
In closing, I want to say that I heartily support the measure which is now before the committee. I feel that one of the finest things this government can do is to increase the amount available for lending under the Farm Improvement Loans Act.

Farm Improvement Loans Act

I shall try not to make too long an outburst at this time, but I should like to spend a lew minutes, with the permission of the hon. member for Laurier and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, in speaking to this measure. This act has proven quite successful in my community. The farmers are using the farm improvement loans to a great extent. They are not having any trouble with the bank. We see the machinery companies charging 11 per cent interest. In most instances when farmers go to these machinery companies their credit is not too good at the banks.
We must admit that we are handling a great deal of the people's money because the government is guaranteeing these loans to the banks. It is the bank's responsibility, therefore, to see that they obtain good security before making these loans. In some parts of the province the farmers use the improvement loan to buy cattle. Then, when they have used the loan to buy cattle they find that they need some new machinery. They buy this through the machinery company and they have to pay a high rate of interest. Thank goodness we are living in a free country. It is the farmer's business whether or not he wants to buy his machinery through these machinery companies and pay a high rate of interest. Some people would like to dictate to us in this country and tell us what we should do. We do not want that to take place.
These farmers who use the credit made available by the machinery companies are also protected by life insurance. There is one instance in particular of which I know where the farmer had bought machinery through the credit of the implement company. Even before taking delivery of the combine he was seized with a heart attack. However, through borrowing money in this way his combine was completely paid for and the wife did not have that debt hanging over her head. On the other hand, if the money had been borrowed through the bank she would have been responsible for this liability. I heard the thought mentioned tonight that the provisions of the act should be extended to buying cattle. I understand from the minister and his assistant that this is the case now. I am quite sure that the farmer can buy livestock today with a farm improvement loan.
I do not want to take any more time of the committee tonight. I would say to the minister that this is a very good legislation and that I am sure that it will be appreciated by the farmers of Canada.

Like those who have spoken previously, I do not want to take too much


of the time of the committee tonight. However, I have a few questions that I should like to put to the minister with regard to the mechanics of this act. First I should like to ask the minister what the percentage is of the yearly loss on loans made under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. Has the fund actually cost the people of Canada any money or is the percentage and so on sufficient to carry any losses that have been incurred on the part of the banks? What is the percentage of repossessions? What is the disposition of the balance of the amount owing to the bank? Another question is this. What are the mechanics of the payment from the government to the bank in the case of a bad loan? Is only 10 per cent of the balance paid by the government of Canada or is the entire balance paid by the government of Canada? In the case of a bad loan, what happens when there is a compromise offered by an estate or a brother who may want to take over a loan from one of the family who through illness or some other reason cannot carry on with the commitment? Is there any provision in the act whereby a compromise can be entertained by the bank or by the government? I think those are some of the questions that some of the farmers want answered.

speechtext:
I have one matter to bring before the committee on the introduction of this resolution with regard to the Farm Improvement Loans Act. While I am on my feet I should also like to state that I believe the restrictions in the terms of the act should be lessened somewhat. I am thinking particularly of the younger people in my area who wish to go on a farm but who find it necessary to become involved in other occupations until such time as they are eligible for this type of support or other loans that may be available to them. I think a broadening of the basis of such loans is warranted because of the record of these payments. When one considers the insignificant amount of money that is lost in the lending process under the act, namely one tenth of 1 per cent. I think the minister could take a broader look at the terms and assist the type of person to which I have made reference.
There is one other important point in relation to these loans which I think should be mentioned. Through experience of the last few years I have seen instances in which the farmer has become indebted through one of these loans on the purchase of machinery and has sustained loss by reason of a fire on his property. In many cases, if his ability to earn money on the farm is greatly limited or restricted, he will not of his own accord procure insurance in order to cover that machinery which has been purchased. Consequently when such a loss is sustained by him, it is

multiplied owing to the fact that he has not seen fit to pay for insurance on this equipment.
I think the minister might also take a look at the possibility of requiring insurance to be placed on such machinery when the loan is made at the bank. On looking at the record of the act over the years, one can see that, having regard to the amount of money that has been loaned, the loss through default has been low. As I stated, the record of repayment is one which I stress again. It has been such that I think the minister might consider broadening the basis on which loans are made particularly, as I have stated, to younger farmers and as a previous speaker pointed out, on the basis of loans for livestock. The risk is very small and it would put a substantial number of these younger farmers on a much more independent basis.

-in legislation of this importance which affects so many veterans across Canada. In the fall of 1957, when certain major changes were being made in the War Veterans Allowance Act, I noticed that the house took about two days discussing the resolution stage, and then a considerable time on second reading. I presume that with a measure of this importance a somewhat similar course of action will be followed this year.
The reason is obvious. There is no hon. member of the House of Commons who is not interested in the problems that affect war veterans. Every province in Canada has its quota of war veterans and there is a great deal of interest by the public generally in the care and attention which is provided by the parliament of Canada for the veterans of former wars.
The War Veterans Allowance Act has been in effect since the year 1930. It was brought in at that time in recognition of something that was known to veterans of the first world war, of the South African war and of the northwest rebellion of 1885, that many men who served in the campaigns of those wars, although not wounded and not eligible for

Business of the House
pension, nevertheless as a result of the hardships they underwent and the exposure to the elements suffered in a way which made it difficult for them in later years to reestablish themselves effectively in society and to continue to earn a living.
Experience has shown that when veterans who have undergone campaigns have reached the age of 60 years or thereabouts they may enter upon rather difficult times whether or not they have been wounded. Therefore the legislation introduced in 1930 was designed to provide some assistance to veterans in that particular category.
During the 30 years this act has been in operation 158,867 veterans and 28,075 widows and orphans have been given assistance. At the present time there are 47,204 veterans on the roll and 19,266 dependents.
The annual charge has risen over the years. I spoke on this subject in the House of Commons on March 7, 1955. At that time 1 reviewed the number of people who were on the war veterans allowance roll. At that particular period the sum of money that was voted by parliament was close to $27 million. Over the years it has increased and in the fiscal year 1956-57 the annual charge was, in round figures, $41 million. In the fiscal year 1959-60 the charge was $57 million.
This gives hon. members an indication of the cost of war veterans allowance over the years and as I continue my remarks tomorrow I will give further details concerning the background of this very useful legislation. I do not know of any piece of legislation apart from the Disabled Persons Act which is more acceptable to veterans across Canada.
